Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $m,\hbar>0$, put
$c:=2\pi^{2}\hbar^{2}/m$, and let $H_{0}$ be the free operator of
[[thm-nrqm-composites-real-multipliers-and-free-bounded-potential-operators]]
clause (b) with $d=3$, this $c$ and $b=0$:
$$H_{0}:=\mathcal F_{2}^{*}M_{c|\xi|^{2}}\mathcal F_{2},\qquad D(H_{0}):=\bigl\{f\in L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C):|\xi|^{2}\mathcal F_{2}f\in L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C)\bigr\},$$
where $\mathcal F_{2}$ is the unitary Plancherel transform of that theorem.
Let $D^{2}_{j}$ denote the second weak partial derivative in the $j$-th
coordinate, defined componentwise on the locally integrable classes of
$\mathbb R^{3}$ ([[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]),
write $\Delta_{w}:=D^{2}_{1}+D^{2}_{2}+D^{2}_{3}$ for the weak Laplacian
(defined on the classes whose three second weak partial derivatives lie in
$L^{2}$), and let $W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C)$ be the Sobolev space
([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]). Then:

(a) $D(H_{0})=W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C)$ as sets and
$$H_{0}f=-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}\,\Delta_{w}f\qquad\text{for every }f\in D(H_{0});$$
equivalently, $\mathcal F_{2}(H_{0}f)(\xi)=c|\xi|^{2}\mathcal F_{2}f(\xi)$ and
$\mathcal F_{2}\bigl(-\tfrac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}\Delta_{w}f\bigr)(\xi)=c|\xi|^{2}\mathcal F_{2}f(\xi)$
for almost every $\xi$, and the two $L^{2}$ classes agree.

(b) For every real bounded measurable $V:\mathbb R^{3}\to\mathbb R$, the
operator $H_{0}+M_{V}$ of clause (c) of the cited theorem, with domain
$D(H_{0})$, coincides with the operator $f\mapsto-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}\Delta_{w}f+Vf$
on the same domain; in particular, for $E\in\mathbb R$ and
$\psi\in W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C)$ the eigenvalue equation
$(H_{0}+M_{V})\psi=E\psi$ is equivalent to the weak equation
$-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}\Delta_{w}\psi+V\psi=E\psi$ elementwise in
$L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C)$.

The statement identifies operators on the same domain; it asserts neither
smoothness of the classes in $W^{2,2}$ nor any physical interpretation.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]), let $d\ge1$ and work on the complex Hilbert space $H=L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$, whose completeness follows from [[thm-riesz-fischer-completeness-of-l-p]] and whose Hilbert-space structure is defined in [[def-hilbert-space]].

(a) For a real measurable finite-valued function $a:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ define $M_af:=af$ on $D(M_a):=\{f\in H: af\in H\}$. Then $M_a$ is a densely defined self-adjoint operator on $H$ ([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]).

(b) Let $c>0$, $b\in\mathbb R$, and let $\mathcal F_2$ be the unitary Plancherel transform with the convention $\widehat f(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}dx$ on $L^1$ ([[def-fourier-transform-on-l-one-of-rn]], [[thm-plancherel]]). Define

$$H_0:=\mathcal F_2^*\,M_{c|\xi|^2+b}\,\mathcal F_2,\qquad D(H_0):=\{f\in H:|\xi|^2\mathcal F_2f\in H\}.$$

Then $H_0$ is self-adjoint, $D(H_0)$ coincides with the Sobolev space $W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ as a set (with equivalent norms, [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[thm-fourier-characterisation-of-integer-order-hilbert-sobolev-spaces]]), $H_0\ge b$ in the quadratic-form sense, and for every Schwartz function $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, $H_0f=-(c/4\pi^2)\Delta f+bf$.

(c) If $V:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ is measurable with $\|V\|_\infty<\infty$ and $H:=H_0+M_V$ with domain $D(H_0)$, then $H$ is self-adjoint on $D(H_0)$, is bounded below, and the assignment $t\mapsto e^{itH}$ is a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group whose generator is $iH$: the limit $\lim_{t\to0}\frac1t(e^{itH}\psi-\psi)$ exists exactly for $\psi\in D(H)$ and equals $iH\psi$ ([[lem-self-adjoint-operator-generates-a-strongly-continuous-unitary-group]]).

(d) *Scope*: the argument uses only boundedness and measurability of $V$; it proves nothing for $V\propto-1/|x|$, $V\propto|x|^2$ or the delta interaction, does not identify $H_0$ with any measured free-particle Hamiltonian, and asserts no physical interpretation.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be a
complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]), let $A:D(A)\subset H\to H$ be a
densely defined self-adjoint operator
([[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]],
[[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]]), and let $c>0$ be
real. Write $cA$ for the operator with domain $D(cA):=D(A)$ and
$(cA)x:=c\,(Ax)$. Then:

(a) $cA$ is self-adjoint.

(b) For every $z\in\mathbb C$ one has $z\in\rho(cA)$ if and only if
$z/c\in\rho(A)$, and then
$(cA-z)^{-1}=c^{-1}(A-z/c)^{-1}$; consequently
$\rho(cA)=c\,\rho(A)$ and $\sigma(cA)=c\,\sigma(A)$.

(c) If some, hence every, resolvent of $A$ is compact
([[def-resolvent-and-spectrum-of-a-closed-unbounded-operator]],
[[def-compact-linear-operator]]), then every resolvent of $cA$ is compact and
$A$ and $cA$ have the same complete orthonormal eigenfamily $(e_j)_{j\in J}$.
If $N:=\dim H<\infty$, take $J=\{1,\ldots,N\}$; if $H$ is infinite dimensional,
take $J=\mathbb N$, with $|\mu_j|\to\infty$ and each eigenvalue repeated
according to its finite multiplicity. In both cases $Ae_j=\mu_je_j$,
$(cA)e_j=c\mu_je_j$, and
$$\sigma(A)=\{\mu_j:j\in J\},\qquad\sigma(cA)=\{c\mu_j:j\in J\}$$
with no other spectral points. The finite-dimensional conclusion also holds
without a separate compactness assumption, since bounded operators on such
$H$ are compact.

(d) Eigenvectors correspond exactly: for $\lambda\in\mathbb R$ and $x\in H$,
$x\ne0$, one has $x\in D(A)$ and $Ax=\lambda x$ if and only if
$x\in D(cA)$ and $(cA)x=(c\lambda)x$; and every eigenvalue of $cA$ has the same
eigenspace as the corresponding eigenvalue of $A$.

(e) If $A\ge\gamma$ in the quadratic-form sense, meaning that
$\langle Ax,x\rangle\ge\gamma\|x\|^2$ for every $x\in D(A)$, then
$cA\ge c\gamma$ in the same sense.

Only the scaling of the given operator is asserted; no domain, spectrum or
eigenvector is claimed for any other rescaling, and no physical
interpretation is attached.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on the nonzero
complex Hilbert space $H$. Then there is a unique regular projection valued
measure $E$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$ such that
$$
D(T)=\Bigl\{x\in H:\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,dE_x(\lambda)<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad Tx=\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE(\lambda)x\quad(x\in D(T)).
$$
Conversely, if $E$ is a regular projection valued measure on $\mathbb R$, then
the operator $\int\lambda\,dE$ with that domain is self-adjoint and its
spectral projection valued measure is $E$ again.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space
([[def-measurable-space]], [[def-sigma-algebra]]) and let $H$ be a complex
Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). A **projection valued measure** (PVM) on
$(X,\Sigma)$ is a map

$$E:\Sigma\longrightarrow\mathcal B(H),\qquad B\longmapsto E(B),$$

such that:

1. $E(B)$ is an **orthogonal projection** for every $B\in\Sigma$, that is, a
   bounded operator with $E(B)^2=E(B)=E(B)^*$; there is no finite-dimensional
   restriction;
2. $E(\varnothing)=0$ and $E(X)=I$;
3. $E(B\cap C)=E(B)E(C)$ for all $B,C\in\Sigma$;
4. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(B_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\Sigma$ with
   union $B$ and every $x\in H$, the series $\sum_nE(B_n)x$ converges in norm
   to $E(B)x$, that is
   $$E(B)x=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}E(B_n)x .$$

Clause 4 is **strong countable additivity**. A PVM is called **regular** when
$X$ is a locally compact Hausdorff space ([[def-locally-compact-space]]), the
$\sigma$-algebra is the Borel $\sigma$-algebra, and every one of the finite
positive measures

$$E_x(B):=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle,\qquad x\in H,\ B\in\Sigma,$$

is a regular Borel measure ([[def-regular-borel-measure-on-an-lch-space]]). Inner
products are linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]); this fixed convention is the one
used for every pairing $E_{x,y}(B)=\langle E(B)x,y\rangle$ on this page.

**Well-definedness: the projection clause.** The conditions $P^2=P=P^*$ are
simultaneously meaningful and describe exactly the Hilbert orthogonal
projections, with no hidden finite-dimensional hypothesis. Indeed, for a
bounded $P$ with $P^2=P=P^*$ the range $\operatorname{ran}P$ is a linear
subspace, and for $y=Pw$ one has
$\langle x-Px,y\rangle=\langle P(x-Px),w\rangle=\langle Px-P^2x,w\rangle=0$, so
$x-Px\perp\operatorname{ran}P$; conversely $\langle Pz,Pz\rangle=\langle z,P^*Pz\rangle=\langle z,Pz\rangle=0$
for $z\perp\operatorname{ran}P$, so $z\in\ker P$, while
$\langle z,Px\rangle=\langle Pz,x\rangle=0$ for $z\in\ker P$ gives
$\ker P=(\operatorname{ran}P)^\perp$
([[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]],
[[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Hence
$\operatorname{ran}P=(\ker P)^\perp$ is closed, and the two defining properties
$Px\in\operatorname{ran}P$, $x-Px\in(\operatorname{ran}P)^\perp$ of
[[def-hilbert-orthogonal-projection]] show that $P=P_{\operatorname{ran}P}$ is
the Hilbert orthogonal projection onto a closed subspace, and conversely every
such $P_M$ is idempotent and self-adjoint by
[[lem-orthogonal-projection-is-linear-self-adjoint-contractive]] and
[[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]]. Finally $P$ is
contractive: from $\langle Px,x\rangle=\langle Px,Px\rangle=\|Px\|^2$ and
Cauchy–Schwarz, $\|Px\|^2\le\|Px\|\,\|x\|$, so $\|Px\|\le\|x\|$ for all $x$,
and $\langle Px,x\rangle=\|Px\|^2\ge0$ is a nonnegative real number.

**Well-definedness: the regularity clause.** For an orthogonal projection value
the pairing $E_x(B)=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle$ is a nonnegative real number and
$E_x(X)=\langle x,x\rangle=\|x\|^2<+\infty$, so every $E_x$ is a finite
nonnegative set function and the regularity requirement is a meaningful
condition on it; that each $E_x$ is genuinely a countably additive measure of
total mass $\|x\|^2$, and that the polarized pairings $E_{x,y}$ are finite
complex measures, is proved as
[[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]] before either is used.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space, let $H$ be a
nonzero complex Hilbert space, let $E$ be a projection valued measure on
$(X,\Sigma)$, and let $f:X\to\mathbb C$ be bounded and $\Sigma$-measurable
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]). Then:

1. there is a unique operator $\Phi_E(f)\in\mathcal B(H)$ with
   $$\langle\Phi_E(f)x,y\rangle=\int f\,dE_{x,y}\qquad(x,y\in H),$$
   and for every sequence $(s_n)$ of complex simple functions with
   $\|f-s_n\|_\infty\to0$ one has $\|\Phi_E(f)-\int s_n\,dE\|\to0$: the integral
   is obtained from uniform simple approximations and is independent of the
   approximating sequence;
2. $\|\Phi_E(f)\|\le\|f\|_\infty$, and for every $x\in H$
$$\langle\Phi_E(f)x,x\rangle=\int f\,dE_x,\qquad \|\Phi_E(f)x\|^2=\int|f|^2\,dE_x ;$$
3. the exact norm is the **$E$-essential supremum**
$$\|f\|_{E,\infty}:=\sup\bigl\{\|f\|_{\infty,E_x}:\ x\in H,\ \|x\|=1\bigr\}, \qquad \|\Phi_E(f)\|=\|f\|_{E,\infty},$$
   where $\|f\|_{\infty,E_x}$ denotes the essential supremum of the real measurable function $|f|$ with respect to
   the finite measure $E_x$ ([[def-essential-supremum-with-respect-to-a-measure]]).

Assume Countable Choice. Let $E$ be a projection valued measure on the
measurable space $(X,\Sigma)$ acting on the complex Hilbert space $H$
([[def-projection-valued-measure]]), and let $f:X\to\mathbb C$ be
$\Sigma$-measurable. Put
$$D(f(E)):=\Bigl\{x\in H:\int_X|f|^2\,dE_x<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad E_x(B)=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle,$$
where the scalar measures $E_x$ are those of
[[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]], and for $x\in D(f(E))$ set
$$f(E)x:=\lim_{n\to\infty}\Phi_E\bigl(f\,\mathbf 1_{\{|f|\le n\}}\bigr)x,$$
For $H\ne\{0\}$, the bounded integrals $\Phi_E$ are those of
[[thm-bounded-borel-pvm-integral]], and the limit is taken in the norm of $H$.
For $H=\{0\}$, define $\Phi_E(g)$ to be the unique operator on $H$ for every bounded measurable $g$. Then $E_0$ is the zero measure, $D(f(E))=H$, and $f(E)0=0$. Thus this case is defined directly without applying a theorem requiring a nonzero space.

**Well-definedness.** $D(f(E))$ is a linear subspace: the estimate
$E_{x+y}\le2E_x+2E_y$ for scalar measures and $E_{\alpha x}=|\alpha|^2E_x$
follow from $\|E(B)(x+y)\|^2\le2\|E(B)x\|^2+2\|E(B)y\|^2$ and
$\|E(B)\alpha x\|^2=|\alpha|^2\|E(B)x\|^2$. Writing $f_n:=f\mathbf 1_{\{|f|\le n\}}$
the sets $\{|f|\le n\}$ are measurable, so $f_n$ is bounded and measurable.
For $m,n\ge N$,
$$|f_n-f_m|^2\le |f|^2\mathbf1_{\{|f|>N\}}.$$
The integral of the right side against $E_x$ tends to zero by
[[thm-dominated-convergence]], with the integrable majorant $|f|^2$ and
pointwise limit zero since $f$ is finite-valued. Linearity of the bounded
calculus ([[thm-pvm-integral-is-a-star-homomorphism]]) and its quadratic identity give
$$\|\Phi_E(f_n)x-\Phi_E(f_m)x\|^2=\int|f_n-f_m|^2\,dE_x.$$
These clauses hold directly on the zero space as well. Hence the truncation
vectors are Cauchy and converge uniquely by Hilbert-space completeness
([[def-hilbert-space]]). The limit is linear in $x$ because every truncation
operator is linear and addition and scalar multiplication are norm-continuous.
Countable Choice is inherited from the bounded PVM suppliers; no further
choice is needed to take these specified limits.

Finally, if two $\Sigma$-measurable functions $f,g$ agree outside a measurable
set $N$ with $E(N)=0$, then $E_x(N)=\|E(N)x\|^2=0$ for every $x$. Thus the
integrals of $|f|^2$ and $|g|^2$ agree, so their domains agree. At every
truncation level their bounded truncations agree outside $N$; the quadratic
identity applied to the difference gives equal truncation vectors for every
$x$. Taking limits gives $f(E)x=g(E)x$ on their common domain.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $E$ be a projection valued measure on $(X,\Sigma)$
on the complex Hilbert space $H$ and let $f:X\to\mathbb C$ be $\Sigma$-measurable. Then the
operator $f(E)$ of [[def-unbounded-integral-against-a-pvm]] is densely defined
and closed, and it is normal, in the sense $D(f(E))=D(f(E)^*)$ and equal norms for the operator and its adjoint; in particular $D(f(E))=D(\overline f(E))$ and
$\|f(E)x\|=\|\overline f(E)x\|$ for all such $x$. Moreover
$$\|f(E)x\|^2=\int|f|^2\,dE_x,\qquad \langle x,f(E)x\rangle=\int\overline f\,dE_x\qquad(x\in D(f(E))),$$
and $(f(E))^*=\overline f(E)$; in particular $f(E)$ is self-adjoint whenever
$f$ takes real values. Finally, if $(g_n)$ are bounded $\Sigma$-measurable functions with
$|g_n|\le C|f|$ pointwise and $g_n\to f$ pointwise, then $g_n(E)x\to f(E)x$
for every $x\in D(f(E))$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on $H$ with
spectral projection valued measure $E$, and set
$U(t):=e^{itT}=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{it\lambda}\,dE(\lambda)$ for $t\in\mathbb R$.
Then $U$ is a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group,
$U(t)D(T)=D(T)$ and $TU(t)=U(t)T$ on $D(T)$, and the derivative
$\lim_{t\to0}\frac1t(U(t)x-x)$ exists exactly for $x\in D(T)$, where it equals
$iTx$. Thus the generator of $U$ is $G=iT$, with $D(G)=D(T)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator with spectral
projection valued measure $E$ on $\mathbb R$ acting on a complex Hilbert space $H$
([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]) and let
$f,g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be Borel. Write $u(T)=u(E)$, with the truncation definition below. If $H=\{0\}$, use its unique PVM and unique full-domain operator directly. Then:

1. $f(T)^*=\overline f(T)$;
2. $f(T)g(T)$ has domain $D(g(T))\cap D((fg)(T))$ and equals the restriction of
   $(fg)(T)$ to that domain, and its closure is $(fg)(T)$;
3. on $D(f(T))\cap D(g(T))$ the sum $f(T)+g(T)$ equals the restriction of
   $(f+g)(T)$, and the closure of $f(T)+g(T)$ is $(f+g)(T)$;
4. the spectrum of $f(T)$ is the essential range
   $\{z\in\mathbb C:E(f^{-1}(B_\varepsilon(z)))\ne0$ for every
   $\varepsilon>0\}$ of $f$ with respect to $E$;
5. if $f$ is continuous then that essential range is the closure of
   $f(\sigma(T))$, with the closure redundant when $f(\sigma(T))$ is closed.

Let $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$ be measurable and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), let $c$ be a nonzero real and write
$cE := \{\, cx : x \in E \,\}$ for $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, where
$(cx)_i := cx_i$. Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(cE) = |c|^{\,n}\,\lambda_n^*(E)$ for every subset $E$, the
   product being defined in $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ because $|c|^{\,n} > 0$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $cE$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(cE) = |c|^{\,n}\lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

At $c = -1$ the map is reflection in the origin and $|c|^{\,n} = 1$, so it
preserves outer measure, measurability and measure. The value $c = 0$ is
excluded because $0E$ is $\{0\}$ or $\varnothing$ and carries no information
about $E$.

derivations.claim: Applying [F1] with $m=1/2$, $\hbar=1$ gives $c_{0}=4\pi^{2}$ and shows that $A_{0}=\mathcal F_{2}^{*}M_{4\pi^{2}|\xi|^{2}}\mathcal F_{2}$ is self-adjoint with $D(A_{0})=W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C)$ and $A_{0}f=-\Delta_{w}f$.

Multiplying by $c>0$, [F3] clause (a) makes $cA_0=H_0$ self-adjoint on $D(A_0)$, and [F1] identifies its action with $-\hbar^2\Delta_w/(2m)$. Since $W=V/c$ and $c\ne0$, the maximal multiplier domains satisfy $D(M_W)=D(M_V)$; the assumed inclusion $D(A_0)\subseteq D(M_V)$ makes both sums well defined on the common domain. The operator $A=A_0+M_W$ is self-adjoint there by hypothesis, and [F3] makes $H=cA$ self-adjoint on that same domain. For $f\in D(A_0)$, $cAf=cA_0f+cWf=cA_0f+Vf$, proving (a). If $V$ is bounded, $M_V$ is bounded on all $L^2$ and [F2] proves the assumed self-adjointness of $A$ automatically; this retains the original branch.

Put $m_c(\lambda)=c\lambda$ and, for Borel $B$, $F(B):=E_A(m_c^{-1}(B))=E_A(B/c)$. Preimages preserve intersections and countable disjoint unions, so [F4] gives the projection, identity and strong countable-additivity axioms for $F$. For every $x$, $F_x(B)=E_{A,x}(B/c)$. This scalar measure is regular: a compact $K\subseteq B/c$ approximating $E_{A,x}(B/c)$ transports to the compact $cK\subseteq B$ with the same measure, and an open $U\supseteq B/c$ with arbitrarily small excess transports to the open $cU\supseteq B$ with the same excess. These follow from regularity of $E_{A,x}$ and the homeomorphism $m_c$. Thus $F$ is a regular PVM, with the preimage direction appropriate to scaling $A$ by $c$.

Let $\psi,y\in L^{2}$. If $\lim_{\tau\to+\infty}F(\tau)\psi=y$, then for $\epsilon>0$ there is $S$ with $\|F(\tau)\psi-y\|<\epsilon$ for $\tau>S$; since $\tau(t)=\hbar t/(2m)\to+\infty$ as $t\to+\infty$, there is $T$ with $\tau(t)>S$ for $t>T$, so $\|F(\tau(t))\psi-y\|<\epsilon$ for $t>T$. Conversely, if $\lim_{t\to+\infty}F(\tau(t))\psi=y$, let $\epsilon>0$ and $T$ with $\|F(\tau(t))\psi-y\|<\epsilon$ for $t>T$; for $\tau>\tau(T)$ the inverse $\tau\mapsto2m\tau/\hbar$ gives $t(\tau)>T$, so $\|F(\tau)\psi-y\|<\epsilon$. The case $t,\tau\to-\infty$ is identical with reversed inequalities.

For a complex simple function $g=\sum_k a_k\mathbf1_{B_k}$, $\Phi_F(g)=\sum_k a_kE_A(B_k/c)=\Phi_{E_A}(g\circ m_c)$, since $\mathbf1_{B_k/c}(\lambda)=\mathbf1_{B_k}(c\lambda)$. For bounded Borel $g$, choose simple $g_n$ uniformly approaching $g$; then $g_n\circ m_c$ approaches $g\circ m_c$ uniformly, and [F5] gives $\Phi_F(g)=\Phi_{E_A}(g\circ m_c)$ by operator-norm limits. In particular $\|\Phi_F(g)x\|^2=\int|g|^2dF_x=\int|g(c\lambda)|^2dE_{A,x}(\lambda)$ for every $x$.

Let $g_n(\lambda):=\lambda\mathbf1_{\{|\lambda|\le n\}}$. Step 2.1 gives $\Phi_F(g_n)=\Phi_{E_A}\bigl(c\lambda\mathbf1_{\{|c\lambda|\le n\}}\bigr)$; the cutoff is $|c\lambda|\le n$, not $|\lambda|\le n$. Its squared-norm identity and [F7] applied to the increasing squared cutoffs give $\int\lambda^2dF_x=c^2\int\lambda^2dE_{A,x}$, including possibly infinite values, for every $x$. Thus the identity-integral domain for $F$ is exactly $D(A)$ by [F4], [F5]. On that domain, the bounded functions $k_n(\lambda):=\lambda\mathbf1_{\{|c\lambda|\le n\}}$ approach $\lambda$ pointwise and satisfy $|k_n|\le|\lambda|$, so the actual cutoff-convergence clause of [F5] gives $\Phi_{E_A}(k_n)x\to Ax$. Therefore $\int\lambda\,dF\,x=\lim_n\Phi_F(g_n)x=c\lim_n\Phi_{E_A}(k_n)x=cAx$. The domain and action both match $cA$.

By steps 1.3 and 3.1, the identity integral of the regular PVM $F$ equals $cA=H$ on exactly $D(A)$. The converse and uniqueness clauses of [F4] therefore give $E_H=F$, namely $E_H(B)=E_A(B/c)$, equivalently $E_H(cB)=E_A(B)$. Running the same argument for the self-adjoint free operator $A_0$ gives $E_{H_0}(cB)=E_{A_0}(B)$. Scalar pairings yield $\mu^H_\psi(cB)=\mu^A_\psi(B)$, and [F3] clause (b) gives $\sigma(H)=c\sigma(A)$ and $\sigma(H_0)=c\sigma(A_0)$, proving (b).

By [F7], $m_c$ and its inverse preserve Lebesgue null sets. Step 4.1 transports each scalar measure by this bijection, so a measure vanishes on every null set exactly when its counterpart does; a measure supported on a null set transports to one supported on the scaled null set, and conversely. Point masses satisfy $\mu^H_\psi(\{\lambda\})=\mu^A_\psi(\{\lambda/c\})$, so absence of atoms is preserved as well. On the common domain, $H\psi=cA\psi$ makes $H\psi=\lambda\psi$ equivalent to $A\psi=(\lambda/c)\psi$ for $\psi\ne0$, proving (e).

For $t\in\mathbb R$ put $\tau=\hbar t/(2m)$, so that $t\lambda/\hbar=\tau\mu$ with $\lambda=c\mu$; by [F6] and the bounded case of 2.1 applied to the bounded measurable function $g(\lambda)=e^{-it\lambda/\hbar}=e^{-i\tau\lambda/c}$ one has $e^{-itH/\hbar}=\int e^{-it\lambda/\hbar}\,dE_{H}(\lambda)=\int e^{-i\tau\mu}\,dE_{A}(\mu)=e^{-i\tau A}$, and the same identity with $H_{0},A_{0}$ gives the second display of (c).

With $F(\tau):=e^{i\tau A}e^{-i\tau A_{0}}$ and $G(t):=e^{itH/\hbar}e^{-itH_{0}/\hbar}$, step 5.2 gives $G(t)=F(\tau(t))$ for every $t$; so step 1.4 shows that the strong limits $\operatorname*{s-lim}_{t\to\pm\infty}G(t)$ and $\operatorname*{s-lim}_{\tau\to\pm\infty}F(\tau)$ exist exactly together and then coincide. This is (d) and completes the proof.

If $f,g:U\to\mathbb R^n$ are totally differentiable at $a$ and $c\in\mathbb R$, then $f+g$ and $cf$ are totally differentiable at $a$, with

$$D(f+g)(a)=Df(a)+Dg(a),\qquad D(cf)(a)=cDf(a).$$

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

If $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ is totally differentiable at $a$, then $D_vf(a)$ exists for every $v\in\mathbb R^m$ and equals $Df(a)v$. In particular $\partial_jf(a)=Df(a)e_j$, and the matrix of $Df(a)$ is $Jf(a)$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

If every partial derivative $\partial_jf_i(a)$ of $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ exists, the **Jacobian matrix** is $Jf(a)=(\partial_jf_i(a))_{i<n,j<m}$. For scalar-valued $f$, its **gradient** is

$$\nabla f(a):=(\partial_0f(a),\ldots,\partial_{m-1}f(a))\in\mathbb R^m,$$

with coordinates understood in the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(-x)=-\sin x,\qquad\cos(-x)=\cos x,\qquad\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.$$
Consequently $|\sin x|\le1$ and $|\cos x|\le1$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{n-1}):U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$ in the componentwise Euclidean sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Then the **divergence** of $F$ is $\operatorname{div}F:=\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i$, the function $U\to\mathbb R$ whose value at $p$ is $\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i(p)$. The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and the sum is the finite sum used throughout [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Since each $\partial_iF_i$ is continuous on $U$, so is $\operatorname{div}F$.

Now let $n=3$ and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$. Following [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], write the three coordinates of a point and of a vector as $x,y,z$ rather than $0,1,2$, so that $F=(F_x,F_y,F_z)$ means $F=(F_0,F_1,F_2)$ and $\partial_x,\partial_y,\partial_z$ are $\partial_0,\partial_1,\partial_2$. With that naming, the **curl** of $F$ is $\operatorname{curl}F:=(\partial_yF_z-\partial_zF_y,\ \partial_zF_x-\partial_xF_z,\ \partial_xF_y-\partial_yF_x)$, a map $U\to\mathbb R^3$ each of whose coordinates is continuous on $U$. In this naming the divergence reads $\operatorname{div}F=\partial_xF_x+\partial_yF_y+\partial_zF_z$.

Both operators are defined pointwise from the first partial derivatives of the components, so no differentiability of $F$ beyond $C^1$ is used and no orientation or metric structure enters beyond the standard coordinates of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. For a $C^1$ scalar function $f$ on $U$, the gradient $\nabla f=(\partial_0f,\ldots,\partial_{n-1}f)$ is that of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]; in the three-coordinate naming, $\nabla f=(\partial_xf,\partial_yf,\partial_zf)$.

If every partial derivative $\partial_jf_i(a)$ of $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ exists, the **Jacobian matrix** is $Jf(a)=(\partial_jf_i(a))_{i<n,j<m}$. For scalar-valued $f$, its **gradient** is

$$\nabla f(a):=(\partial_0f(a),\ldots,\partial_{m-1}f(a))\in\mathbb R^m,$$

with coordinates understood in the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F,G:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$, let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$ and let $a,b\in\mathbb R$. Then $aF+bG$ and $fF$ are $C^1$ on $U$ and

$$\operatorname{div}(aF+bG)=a\operatorname{div}F+b\operatorname{div}G,$$

$$\operatorname{div}(fF)=\langle\nabla f,F\rangle+f\operatorname{div}F.$$

If moreover $n=3$, then

$$\operatorname{curl}(aF+bG)=a\operatorname{curl}F+b\operatorname{curl}G,\qquad \operatorname{curl}(fF)=\nabla f\times F+f\operatorname{curl}F.$$

Here $\operatorname{div}$, $\operatorname{curl}$ and the coordinate naming are those of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], $\nabla f$ is the gradient of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ is the inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and $\times$ is the cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]].

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For $n\ge2$, a bounded $C^1$ domain Omega and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$, $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F\,dx=\int_{\partial\Omega}F\cdot\nu\,dS$. Both integrals are finite, with the continuous interior derivative convention and the outward normal on every boundary component.

derivations.claim: By [F1], $\partial_{t}n=\partial_{t}(u^{2}+v^{2})=2(u\,\partial_{t}u+v\,\partial_{t}v)$ pointwise on $\Omega\times I$.

Put $F:=u
abla v-v
abla u$. By [F2] applied to each of the two products, using $\operatorname{div}(
abla v)=\sum_{i=0}^{2}\partial_{i}\partial_{i}v=\Delta v$ and likewise for $u$, one has $\operatorname{div}(u
abla v)=
abla u\cdot
abla v+u\,\Delta v$ and $\operatorname{div}(v
abla u)=
abla v\cdot
abla u+v\,\Delta u$; the mixed terms are equal by symmetry of the inner product and cancel in the difference, so $\operatorname{div}F=u\,\Delta v-v\,\Delta u$ and hence $\operatorname{div}\mathbf j= rac{\hbar}{m}(u\Delta v-v\Delta u)$.

Reading the complex equation $i\hbar\partial_{t}(u+iv)=-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}\Delta(u+iv)+V(u+iv)$ by real and imaginary parts gives $\hbar\,\partial_{t}u=-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}\Delta v+Vv$ and $-\hbar\,\partial_{t}v=-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}\Delta u+Vu$, i.e. $\partial_{t}u=-\frac{\hbar}{2m}\Delta v+\frac{V}{\hbar}v$ and $\partial_{t}v=\frac{\hbar}{2m}\Delta u-\frac{V}{\hbar}u$.

For $u=\cos(kd\cdot x)$, $v=\sin(kd\cdot x)$ the chain rule [F1] gives $
abla u=-k\,d\,\sin(kd\cdot x)$ and $
abla v=k\,d\,\cos(kd\cdot x)$; hence $u
abla v-v
abla u=k\,d\,(\cos^{2}+\sin^{2})=k\,d$ and $\mathbf j= rac{\hbar k}{m}d$. The two functions are $C^{\infty}$ and satisfy the stationary equations with $V=0$, because $\partial_{i}\partial_{i}u=-k^{2}d_{i}^{2}\cos(kd\cdot x)$ and $\partial_{i}\partial_{i}v=-k^{2}d_{i}^{2}\sin(kd\cdot x)$ by [F1], so summing over $i=0,1,2$ and using $|d|^{2}=1$ gives $\Delta u=-k^{2}u$ and $\Delta v=-k^{2}v$ with $E=\hbar^{2}k^{2}/(2m)$.

Write $c_{k}:=\cos(kr)$, $s_{k}:=\sin(kr)$ and $f=a+ib$. Then $u=r^{-1}(ac_{k}-bs_{k})$, $v=r^{-1}(as_{k}+bc_{k})$, so by the chain and product rules for functions of the single variable $r$ [F1], $\partial_{r}u=-k\,r^{-1}(as_{k}+bc_{k})-r^{-2}(ac_{k}-bs_{k})$ and $\partial_{r}v=k\,r^{-1}(ac_{k}-bs_{k})-r^{-2}(as_{k}+bc_{k})$. Multiplying out, $u\,\partial_{r}v-v\,\partial_{r}u=k\,r^{-2}\bigl[(ac_{k}-bs_{k})^{2}+(as_{k}+bc_{k})^{2}\bigr]=k\,r^{-2}(a^{2}+b^{2})=k\,r^{-2}|f(\omega)|^{2}$; since $\hat r$ is a unit vector and the radial directional derivative of an angular function is zero, $\mathbf j\cdot\hat r=\frac{\hbar}{m}(u\,\partial_{r}v-v\,\partial_{r}u)$, which is the first display of (c), and multiplying by $r^{2}>0$ gives the equivalent second display. Both $u$ and $v$ are $C^{1}$ on $\Omega$: they are sums of products of the $C^{\infty}$ radial factors $r^{-1}$, $\cos(kr)$, $\sin(kr)$ with the $C^{1}$ angular factors $a,b$, and the radial extensions of $a,b$ are $C^{1}$ by the explicit convention in (c), so the Euclidean product rules give the stated regularity.

Substituting 1.3 into 1.1 and using that $V$ is real, $2(u\partial_{t}u+v\partial_{t}v)=2\bigl(-\frac{\hbar}{2m}u\Delta v+\frac{V}{\hbar}uv+\frac{\hbar}{2m}v\Delta u-\frac{V}{\hbar}vu\bigr)=-\frac{\hbar}{m}(u\Delta v-v\Delta u)$. Adding the value of $\operatorname{div}\mathbf j$ from 1.2 gives $\partial_{t}n+\operatorname{div}\mathbf j=0$, which is (a).

If $u,v,V$ do not depend on $t$ and satisfy the stationary equations, then $\Delta u=\frac{2m}{\hbar^{2}}(V-E)u$ and $\Delta v=\frac{2m}{\hbar^{2}}(V-E)v$ pointwise, so 1.2 gives $\operatorname{div}\mathbf j=\frac{\hbar}{m}\cdot\frac{2m}{\hbar^{2}}(V-E)(uv-vu)=0$ on $\Omega$.

Let $\overline{B(a,r)}\subseteq\Omega$. The ball $B(a,r)$ is a bounded $C^{1}$ domain and $\mathbf j$ is $C^{1}$ on a neighbourhood of its closure, so [F3] gives $\int_{\partial B(a,r)}\mathbf j\cdot\nu\,dS=\int_{B(a,r)}\operatorname{div}\mathbf j\,dx=0$ by 2.2; with 1.4 for the plane-wave reading, 1.5 for the outgoing current identity, 2.1 for (a) and this step for (b), the proof of (a), (b) and (c) is complete.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $m,\hbar>0$, put
$c:=\hbar^{2}/(2m)$, let $\mathcal F_{2}$ be the unitary Plancherel transform of
[[thm-nrqm-composites-real-multipliers-and-free-bounded-potential-operators]]
clause (b) in dimension $d=3$, let $V:\mathbb R^{3}\to\mathbb R$ be measurable
and put $W:=V/c$. For a measurable $U$ let $M_U$ be the maximal
multiplication operator on $L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$, with
$D(M_U):=\{f\in L^2:Uf\in L^2\}$ and $M_Uf:=Uf$. Write
$$A_{0}:=\mathcal F_{2}^{*}M_{4\pi^{2}|\xi|^{2}}\mathcal F_{2},\qquad D(A_{0}):=\bigl\{f\in L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C):|\xi|^{2}\mathcal F_{2}f\in L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C)\bigr\},$$
$$A:=A_{0}+M_{W},\quad D(A):=D(A_{0}),\qquad H_{0}:=cA_{0},\qquad H:=cA=cA_{0}+M_{V}.$$
$D(A_{0})\subseteq D(M_V)=D(M_W)$ is assumed, and assume that
$A=A_0+M_W$ is self-adjoint on $D(A_0)$. These two hypotheses hold
automatically for real bounded measurable $V$ by
[[thm-nrqm-composites-real-multipliers-and-free-bounded-potential-operators]]
clauses (a),(c), so every original bounded-potential case is retained.
So $A_{0}$ is the operator $-\Delta_{w}$ of
[[lem-nrqm-central-free-operator-differential-identification]] and
$D(A_{0})=W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C)$
([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]). For a self-adjoint operator $T$ write
$E_{T}$ for the regular projection valued measure of
[[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]] and
$\mu^{T}_{\psi}(B):=\langle E_{T}(B)\psi,\psi\rangle$ for $\psi\in L^{2}$. Then:

(a) $A$ and $H$ are self-adjoint with domain $D(A)=W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C)$,
and $H=cA$ and $H_{0}=cA_{0}$ hold as operator identities on that common domain;

(b) for every Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb R$,
$$E_{H}(cB)=E_{A}(B),\qquad E_{H_{0}}(cB)=E_{A_{0}}(B);$$
consequently $\mu^{H}_{\psi}(cB)=\mu^{A}_{\psi}(B)$ for every $\psi$ and every
Borel $B$, and $\sigma(H)=c\,\sigma(A)$, $\sigma(H_{0})=c\,\sigma(A_{0})$;

(c) for every $t\in\mathbb R$, with $\tau:=\hbar t/(2m)=\frac{tc}{\hbar}$,
$$e^{-itH/\hbar}=e^{-i\tau A},\qquad e^{-itH_{0}/\hbar}=e^{-i\tau A_{0}},$$
where the exponentials are those of
[[lem-self-adjoint-operator-generates-a-strongly-continuous-unitary-group]];

(d) let $F:\mathbb R\to\mathcal B(L^{2})$ be any family of bounded operators and
$\tau(t):=\hbar t/(2m)$. For every $\psi\in L^{2}$ the strong limit
$\lim_{t\to\pm\infty}F(\tau(t))\psi$ exists if and only if
$\lim_{\tau\to\pm\infty}F(\tau)\psi$ exists, and then the two limits are equal;
in particular
$$\operatorname*{s-lim}_{t\to\pm\infty}e^{itH/\hbar}e^{-itH_{0}/\hbar} =\operatorname*{s-lim}_{\tau\to\pm\infty}e^{i\tau A}e^{-i\tau A_{0}}$$
in the sense that either strong limit exists exactly when the other does, and
then they are equal;

(e) $\mu^{H}_{\psi}$ is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure
if and only if $\mu^{A}_{\psi}$ is, and likewise for singularity with respect
to Lebesgue measure and for absence of atoms; and $\psi\ne0$ is an eigenvector
of $H$ with eigenvalue $\lambda$ if and only if it is an eigenvector of $A$
with eigenvalue $\lambda/c$.

The statement is an operator identity and a statement about spectral measures;
no physical interpretation, no scattering limit and no cross section is
asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$V\in L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R)$ be real, let $H_0=-\Delta$ on
$D(H_0)=W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$, and let $H=H_0+M_V$ be the
self-adjoint operator on $D(H_0)$ of
[[thm-nrqm-controlled-dynamics-l2-potential-infinitesimal-kinetic-bound]] (c).
Then:

(a) For every Schwartz function $\psi$
$$\int_0^\infty\bigl\|Ve^{-itH_0}\psi\bigr\|_2\,dt<\infty,\qquad \int_{-\infty}^0\bigl\|Ve^{-itH_0}\psi\bigr\|_2\,dt<\infty.$$

(b) Consequently the wave operators
$\Omega_\pm:=\operatorname*{s-lim}_{t\to\pm\infty}e^{itH}e^{-itH_0}$ exist as
bounded linear isometries on $L^2(\mathbb R^3)$ by
[[thm-nrqm-controlled-dynamics-cook-domain-criterion]], with
$\Omega_\pm e^{-isH_0}=e^{-isH}\Omega_\pm$ and
$H\Omega_\pm\psi=\Omega_\pm H_0\psi$ for $\psi\in D(H_0)$.

(c) *Free absolute continuity.* $H_0$ has purely absolutely continuous
spectrum: for every $\psi\in L^2$ the scalar spectral measure of $H_0$ is
absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure, with density
$\frac{\sqrt E}{2(2\pi)^3}\int_{S^2}|\mathcal F_2\psi(\frac{\sqrt E}{2\pi}\Omega)|^2d\sigma(\Omega)$
for almost every $E>0$, using any measurable Fourier representative. This nonnegative density lies in $L^1(0,\infty)$ with integral $\|\psi\|_2^2$, and the measure gives zero mass to $\{0\}$ and to $(-\infty,0)$.
Hence $L^2=H_{\mathrm{ac}}(H_0)$.

Assertions about the ranges of $\Omega_\pm$, asymptotic completeness or the
S-matrix are not made here; they are separate theorems
([[thm-nrqm-controlled-dynamics-compact-support-asymptotic-completeness]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and adopt all
hypotheses of
[[thm-nrqm-controlled-dynamics-cook-domain-criterion]], writing its Hilbert
space as $\mathcal H$ and renaming its operators $A_0,A$ as $H_0,H$: these
are self-adjoint operators on $\mathcal H$ with
$D(H_0)\subseteq D(H)$, $D\subseteq D(H_0)$ dense and $e^{-itH_0}$-invariant,
$\int_{\text{half-line}}\|(H-H_0)e^{-itH_0}\psi\|dt<\infty$ for $\psi\in D$,
$t\mapsto(H-H_0)e^{-itH_0}\psi$ norm-continuous for each $\psi\in D$, and
$\Omega_\pm$ the extensions constructed there. Then:

(a) *Intertwining.* $\Omega_\pm e^{-isH_0}=e^{-isH}\Omega_\pm$ for all
$s\in\mathbb R$, as bounded operators on $\mathcal H$.

(b) *Domain and commutation.* $\Omega_\pm D(H_0)\subseteq D(H)$ and
$H\Omega_\pm\psi=\Omega_\pm H_0\psi$ for every $\psi\in D(H_0)$.

(c) *Range invariance.* The closed subspace $\operatorname{ran}\Omega_\pm$
is invariant under $e^{-isH}$ for every $s$, and
$e^{-isH}|_{\operatorname{ran}\Omega_\pm}
=\Omega_\pm e^{-isH_0}\Omega_\pm^{-1}$ in the sense of the isometric
identification $\Omega_\pm:\mathcal H\to\operatorname{ran}\Omega_\pm$.

(d) $\Omega_\pm^*\Omega_\pm=I$, $\|\Omega_\pm\eta\|=\|\eta\|$ for every
$\eta\in\mathcal H$; no surjectivity onto $\mathcal H$ and no identification of
$\operatorname{ran}\Omega_\pm$ with an absolutely continuous subspace is
asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$V\in L^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R)$ be real and compactly supported, let
$k>0$, and let $H=-\Delta+M_V$ on $D(H)=H^2(\mathbb R^3)$; its self-adjointness
for bounded real $V$ is established below by explicit resolvents. Then $k^2$ is not
an eigenvalue of $H$: if $\psi\in H^2(\mathbb R^3)$ satisfies
$-\Delta\psi+V\psi=k^2\psi$, then $\psi=0$.

**(a) Framework data.** Adopt the state and composition postulate P1, the
observable and probability postulate P2, the autonomous-dynamics postulate P4,
the kinematics and massive-particle model postulate P5, the identical-particle
and spin postulate P6, and the preparation and apparatus discipline P7
([[post-nrqm-framework-state-and-composition]],
[[post-nrqm-framework-observable-and-probability]],
[[post-nrqm-framework-autonomous-dynamics]],
[[post-nrqm-framework-nonrelativistic-kinematics-and-massive-particle]],
[[post-nrqm-framework-identical-particles-and-spin]],
[[post-nrqm-framework-preparation-and-apparatus]]). Fix a mass parameter
$m>0$ and a spin label $s=0$, so that the framework's one-particle model
[[def-nrqm-kinematics-framework-massive-spin-s-model]] reads its state space as
$H_{0}=L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C)$ with the pairing linear in the first
argument, its componentwise position family $Q_{1},Q_{2},Q_{3}$, its
componentwise momentum family $P_{1},P_{2},P_{3}$ and the action constant
$\hbar>0$; the spin-zero internal factor carries the trivial representation of
P6. Units are those of [[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]]: position
is read in metres, momentum in $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$, energy and potential
energy in joules, and $\hbar$ in $\mathrm{J\,s}$. Assume the Axiom of
Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice as the choice hypotheses of the cited
mathematical suppliers ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

Choose a reference length $L_*>0$ in metres and put
$$y=x/L_*,\qquad E_*:=\frac{\hbar^2}{2mL_*^2},\qquad T_*:=\hbar/E_*.$$
Here $y$ is dimensionless, $E_*$ is in joules and $T_*$ in seconds.
The unitary coordinate dilation from physical-coordinate $L^2_x$ to
$L^2_y$ is $(D_*f)(y)=L_*^{3/2}f(L_*y)$, with inverse
$(D_*^*g)(x)=L_*^{-3/2}g(x/L_*)$. Lebesgue dilation
([[thm-lebesgue-measure-under-dilations-and-reflections]]) gives its norm
identity, first for simple functions and then by nonnegative approximation.
This convention makes all coordinates and spectral shifts in the tail
criterion below dimensionless; physical stationary equations retain $x$.

**(b) The declared scattering model and its potential classes.** As an
additional model assumption of the pair, adopt the **short-range scattering
model**. Its declared state space is $H_{0}=L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C)$ of
clause (a), with the position and momentum families of that clause. A
**declared short-range potential** of the model is a real-valued measurable
function $V:\mathbb R^{3}\to\mathbb R$ satisfying either

1. *(compact-support class)* $V$ is bounded, $\|V\|_{\infty}<\infty$, and
   $V=0$ almost everywhere outside some ball
   $B_{\mathrm{supp}}:=\{x:|x|\le R_{\mathrm{supp}}\}$ with
   $R_{\mathrm{supp}}<\infty$; or
2. *(resolvent-tail class)* $V=V_{2}+V_{\mathrm b}$ with real
   $V_{2}\in L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3})$ and real bounded $V_{\mathrm b}$, and, with
   the dimensionless reduced potential
   $W_*(y):=V(L_*y)/E_*=W_{*,2}(y)+W_{*,\mathrm b}(y)$ and
   $A_{0,*}:=-\Delta_y^{\mathrm{weak}}$ on $W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^3_y)$,
   the function
$$h_*(r):=\bigl\|M_{W_*}(A_{0,*}-iI)^{-1}\mathbf 1_{\{|y|\ge r\}}\bigr\|,\qquad r\ge0,$$

   $M_V(H^{\mathrm{free}}-iE_*I)^{-1}\mathbf1_{\{|x|\ge L_*r\}}$:
   conjugation by $D_*$ gives exactly the displayed operator. Thus physical
   cutoffs have radius $L_*r$, and integration in physical radius $R$ gives
   $\int_0^\infty h_*(R/L_*)\,dR=L_*\int_0^\infty h_*(r)\,dr$.
   The reference length is fixed as part of this unit convention.

The function $V$ is read as a potential energy in joules; the model asserts no
derivation of $V$ from P5 or from any force law, and an assignment of a
concrete target to $V$ is a tested identification in the sense of clause (iii)
of P7 carrying the corresponding uncertainty. The pure Coulomb potential
$V(x)=-\kappa/|x|$, $\kappa>0$, is **not** in either class: it is a declared
long-range model with its own definition and comparison construction
on this page.

Plancherel transform of
[[thm-nrqm-composites-real-multipliers-and-free-bounded-potential-operators]]
clause (b), $c:=2\pi^{2}\hbar^{2}/m$, and let
$$H^{\mathrm{free}}:=\mathcal F_{2}^{*}M_{c|\xi|^{2}}\mathcal F_{2},\qquad D(H^{\mathrm{free}}):=\bigl\{f\in H_{0}:|\xi|^{2}\mathcal F_{2}f\in H_{0}\bigr\}$$

[[lem-nrqm-central-free-operator-differential-identification]] its domain is
the Sobolev space $W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C)$
([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]) and
$H^{\mathrm{free}}f=-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}\Delta_{w}f$ with $\Delta_{w}$ the
weak Laplacian ([[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]).
For equations in physical coordinates write $A_{0,x}:=-\Delta_x^{\mathrm{weak}}$
and $W_x(x):=2mV(x)/\hbar^2$, so
$H^{\mathrm{free}}=(\hbar^2/2m)A_{0,x}$. Both $A_{0,x}$ and $W_x$
have inverse-square-length units; this energy division alone is not a
spatial nondimensionalization. Stationary items may abbreviate $W_x$ as $W$
(or its central radial profile as $w$), keeping physical $k$ and $r$.
The dimensionless operators instead satisfy
$$D_*H^{\mathrm{free}}D_*^*=E_*A_{0,*},\qquad D_*HD_*^*=E_*(A_{0,*}+M_{W_*}),\qquad W_*(y)=L_*^2W_x(L_*y).$$
Indeed testing the weak derivative definition after $x=L_*y$ gives
$\partial_y^\alpha D_*f=L_*^{|\alpha|}D_*(\partial_x^\alpha f)$ for
$|\alpha|\le2$; applying the inverse dilation gives the converse, so $D_*$
maps the physical Sobolev domain onto the dimensionless one. Multiplication
transforms by direct substitution, proving both operator identities on their
exact domains. The subscript $w$ in $\Delta_w$ above denotes weak derivatives,
not a coordinate or a unit convention.
With $M_V$ the maximal multiplication operator, $D(M_V)=\{f\in L^2:Vf\in L^2\}$ (bounded and everywhere defined in the compact-support class), the **assigned energy observables** of the model with declared
potential $V$ are the free operator $H^{\mathrm{free}}$ and the interacting
operator
$$H:=H^{\mathrm{free}}+M_{V},\qquad D(H):=D(H^{\mathrm{free}}).$$
The declared energy unit is the joule. For the compact-support class,
clause (c) of the cited theorem makes $H$ self-adjoint on $D(H)$ and bounded
below by $-\|V\|_{\infty}$. For the resolvent-tail class,
[[thm-nrqm-controlled-dynamics-resolvent-tail-short-range-completeness]]
(Statement and proof step 1.1) applies to $W_*=W_{*,2}+W_{*,\mathrm b}$:
$\|W_{*,2}\|_2=E_*^{-1}L_*^{-3/2}\|V_2\|_2<\infty$,
$\|W_{*,\mathrm b}\|_\infty=E_*^{-1}\|V_{\mathrm b}\|_\infty<\infty$,

$H^2_y\subseteq D(M_{W_*})$ and self-adjointness of
$A_{0,*}+M_{W_*}$ on $H^2_y=W^{2,2}_y$. The displayed unitary dilation and
positive scaling therefore give $D(H^{\mathrm{free}})\subseteq D(M_V)$
and self-adjointness of $H$ on precisely $W^{2,2}_x$, without assuming
that $V_2$ is bounded. The
model adopts $(H^{\mathrm{free}},\mathrm J)$ and $(H,\mathrm J)$ as assigned
sharp observables in the sense of
[[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]] clause (a), and
reads their flows by [[def-nrqm-autonomous-dynamics-framework-evolution]]
with $U_{\mathrm{free}}(t)=e^{-itH^{\mathrm{free}}/\hbar}$ and
$U(t)=e^{-itH/\hbar}$.

potential $V$ the model declares the **free asymptotic comparison** to be the
pair of strong limits
$$\Omega_{\pm}:=\operatorname*{s-lim}_{t\to\pm\infty}e^{itH/\hbar}e^{-itH^{\mathrm{free}}/\hbar},$$
which are declared **wave operators** of the model when both limits exist, and
declares the **scattering operator** $S:=\Omega_{+}^{*}\Omega_{-}$ when both
exist and $\Omega_{\pm}$ are isometries. The model says that the pair is
**asymptotically complete** for this $V$ when the two ranges agree with the
subspace
$$H_{\mathrm{ac}}(H):=\{\psi\in H_{0}:\mu^{H}_{\psi}\ll\lambda\},$$
where $\mu^{H}_{\psi}(B):=\langle E_{H}(B)\psi,\psi\rangle$ is the scalar
spectral measure of the projection valued measure $E_{H}$ of the self-adjoint
operator $H$, and with
$$H_{\mathrm c}(H):=H_{\mathrm{pp}}(H)^{\perp},\qquad H_{\mathrm{pp}}(H):=\overline{\operatorname{span}}\{\psi\ne0:H\psi=\lambda\psi\ \text{for some }\lambda\in\mathbb R\};$$
here $H_{\mathrm{pp}}(H)$ is the closed linear span of the eigenvectors of $H$.
An **asymptotic free state** of a vector $\psi\in H_{0}$ is a vector
$\psi_{\mathrm{in}}$ such that
$\bigl\|e^{-itH/\hbar}\psi-e^{-itH^{\mathrm{free}}/\hbar}\psi_{\mathrm{in}}\bigr\|\to0$
as $t\to-\infty$; the model reads this limit relation through the
wave-operator identity $\psi=\Omega_{-}\psi_{\mathrm{in}}$ only when the wave
operator exists. These
are declarations of the model under P4; they construct no preparation,
detector or measured count, and no definition of a cross section appears here.

fixes the pair's spin-zero one-particle data, mass, action constant and choice
hypotheses. Clause (b) further adopts the compact-support and resolvent-tail
potential classes as **additional pair-level model assumptions**; neither
class follows from those postulates or from the cited mathematical results.
Clause (c) declares the assigned energy operators and their common domain;
the cited mathematics establishes self-adjointness where stated, including
the resolvent-tail case supplied by the cited mathematical theorem. Clause (d) declares the
comparison and spectral vocabulary without asserting that the limits exist
or are complete. No identification of $m$, $\hbar$ or $V$ with measured data
is asserted. Existence of the limits, completeness of the ranges and every
cross section are separate results of the pair.

derivations.claim: By [F5], the model supplies self-adjointness of $H=H^{\mathrm{free}}+M_V$ on $W^{2,2}$ and its lower bound $-\|V\|_\infty$. By [F1], the reduced operator $A=-\Delta_w+M_W$ is self-adjoint on the same domain and $H=cA$, with $W=2mV/\hbar^2$. Since $V$ is real, bounded and compactly supported, so is $W$, and in particular $W\in L^2(\mathbb R^3)$. Thus [F2] applies to the actual reduced potential $V_0=W$ and this already self-adjoint $A$; Cook existence is not used as a proof of the self-adjointness it presupposes.

For $\psi\in\mathcal S$ put $\tau(t)=\hbar t/(2m)$. By [F1], $Ve^{-itH^{\mathrm{free}}/\hbar}\psi=cW e^{-i\tau(t)A_{0}}\psi$, and by [F2] the function $\tau\mapsto\|We^{-i\tau A_{0}}\psi\|_{2}$ is integrable on $[0,\infty)$; the substitution $t\mapsto\tau(t)$ in the Lebesgue integral of a continuous integrand, [[cor-one-dimensional-change-of-variables-with-absolute-derivative]], gives $\int_{0}^{\infty}\|We^{-i\tau(t)A_{0}}\psi\|_{2}dt=\frac{2m}{\hbar}\int_{0}^{\infty}\|We^{-i\tau A_{0}}\psi\|_{2}d\tau<\infty$, hence the first Cook integral of (a); the negative half-line is identical.

By [F1] the strong limits in physical time exist exactly when the energy-divided limits in [F2] exist and then coincide; [F2] exhibits them, so $\Omega_{\pm}$ of the statement exist as strong limits and are the operators of [F2]. This is (b)'s existence assertion.

Let $\psi\in D(H)$ with $H\psi=\lambda\psi$ and $\lambda>0$. By [F1] $\psi$ is an eigenvector of $A$ with eigenvalue $\lambda/c>0$; [F4] applied with $k=\sqrt{\lambda/c}>0$ gives $\psi=0$. This is (d).

By [F3] the operators of step 1.3 satisfy $\Omega_{\pm}^{*}\Omega_{\pm}=I$, $e^{-isH/\hbar}\Omega_{\pm}=\Omega_{\pm}e^{-isH^{\mathrm{free}}/\hbar}$ (after replacing the energy-divided time by the physical time through the same reparametrisation) and $H\Omega_{\pm}\psi=\Omega_{\pm}H^{\mathrm{free}}\psi$ for $\psi\in D(H^{\mathrm{free}})$. This completes (b).

By [F2] the scalar measures $\mu^{A_{0}}_{\psi}$ are absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure with zero mass at $0$; by [F1] $\mu^{H^{\mathrm{free}}}_{\psi}(B)=\mu^{A_{0}}_{\psi}(c^{-1}B)$, and since multiplication by $c^{-1}>0$ preserves Lebesgue null sets, the transfer preserves absolute continuity and atomlessness, and $\mu^{H^{\mathrm{free}}}_{\psi}(\{0\})=\mu^{A_{0}}_{\psi}(\{0\})=0$; the spectrum is contained in $[0,\infty)$ because $H^{\mathrm{free}}=cA_{0}$ with $A_{0}\ge0$. Hence every vector is absolutely continuous, $H_{\mathrm{ac}}(H^{\mathrm{free}})=H_{0}$, and there are no eigenvectors. This is (c) and completes the proof.

([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $m,\hbar>0$, put
$c:=\hbar^{2}/(2m)$, let $\mathcal F_{2}$ be the unitary Plancherel transform of
[[thm-nrqm-composites-real-multipliers-and-free-bounded-potential-operators]]
clause (b) in dimension $d=3$, let $V:\mathbb R^{3}\to\mathbb R$ be measurable
and put $W:=V/c$. For a measurable $U$ let $M_U$ be the maximal
multiplication operator on $L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$, with
$D(M_U):=\{f\in L^2:Uf\in L^2\}$ and $M_Uf:=Uf$. Write
$$A_{0}:=\mathcal F_{2}^{*}M_{4\pi^{2}|\xi|^{2}}\mathcal F_{2},\qquad D(A_{0}):=\bigl\{f\in L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C):|\xi|^{2}\mathcal F_{2}f\in L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C)\bigr\},$$
$$A:=A_{0}+M_{W},\quad D(A):=D(A_{0}),\qquad H_{0}:=cA_{0},\qquad H:=cA=cA_{0}+M_{V}.$$
$D(A_{0})\subseteq D(M_V)=D(M_W)$ is assumed, and assume that
$A=A_0+M_W$ is self-adjoint on $D(A_0)$. These two hypotheses hold
automatically for real bounded measurable $V$ by
[[thm-nrqm-composites-real-multipliers-and-free-bounded-potential-operators]]
clauses (a),(c), so every original bounded-potential case is retained.
So $A_{0}$ is the operator $-\Delta_{w}$ of
[[lem-nrqm-central-free-operator-differential-identification]] and
$D(A_{0})=W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C)$
([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]). For a self-adjoint operator $T$ write
$E_{T}$ for the regular projection valued measure of
[[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]] and
$\mu^{T}_{\psi}(B):=\langle E_{T}(B)\psi,\psi\rangle$ for $\psi\in L^{2}$. Then:

(a) $A$ and $H$ are self-adjoint with domain $D(A)=W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C)$,
and $H=cA$ and $H_{0}=cA_{0}$ hold as operator identities on that common domain;

(b) for every Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb R$,
$$E_{H}(cB)=E_{A}(B),\qquad E_{H_{0}}(cB)=E_{A_{0}}(B);$$
consequently $\mu^{H}_{\psi}(cB)=\mu^{A}_{\psi}(B)$ for every $\psi$ and every
Borel $B$, and $\sigma(H)=c\,\sigma(A)$, $\sigma(H_{0})=c\,\sigma(A_{0})$;

(c) for every $t\in\mathbb R$, with $\tau:=\hbar t/(2m)=\frac{tc}{\hbar}$,
$$e^{-itH/\hbar}=e^{-i\tau A},\qquad e^{-itH_{0}/\hbar}=e^{-i\tau A_{0}},$$
where the exponentials are those of
[[lem-self-adjoint-operator-generates-a-strongly-continuous-unitary-group]];

(d) let $F:\mathbb R\to\mathcal B(L^{2})$ be any family of bounded operators and
$\tau(t):=\hbar t/(2m)$. For every $\psi\in L^{2}$ the strong limit
$\lim_{t\to\pm\infty}F(\tau(t))\psi$ exists if and only if
$\lim_{\tau\to\pm\infty}F(\tau)\psi$ exists, and then the two limits are equal;
in particular
$$\operatorname*{s-lim}_{t\to\pm\infty}e^{itH/\hbar}e^{-itH_{0}/\hbar} =\operatorname*{s-lim}_{\tau\to\pm\infty}e^{i\tau A}e^{-i\tau A_{0}}$$
in the sense that either strong limit exists exactly when the other does, and
then they are equal;

(e) $\mu^{H}_{\psi}$ is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure
if and only if $\mu^{A}_{\psi}$ is, and likewise for singularity with respect
to Lebesgue measure and for absence of atoms; and $\psi\ne0$ is an eigenvector
of $H$ with eigenvalue $\lambda$ if and only if it is an eigenvector of $A$
with eigenvalue $\lambda/c$.

The statement is an operator identity and a statement about spectral measures;
no physical interpretation, no scattering limit and no cross section is
asserted.

derivations.claim: The declared potential $V$ is real, bounded and supported in $B_{R}$, so $W=V/c$ is real, bounded and supported in the same ball; hence [F2] applies to $W$. By [F1] the model's interacting operator is $H=cA$ with $A=-\Delta_{w}+M_{W}$ on the common domain.

$D(A_{0})\subseteq D(M_V)=D(M_W)$ is assumed, and assume that
$A=A_0+M_W$ is self-adjoint on $D(A_0)$. These two hypotheses hold
automatically for real bounded measurable $V$ by
[[thm-nrqm-composites-real-multipliers-and-free-bounded-potential-operators]]
clauses (a),(c), so every original bounded-potential case is retained.

[[lem-nrqm-central-free-operator-differential-identification]] and
$D(A_{0})=W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C)$
([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]). For a self-adjoint operator $T$ write
$E_{T}$ for the regular projection valued measure of
[[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]] and
$\mu^{T}_{\psi}(B):=\langle E_{T}(B)\psi,\psi\rangle$ for $\psi\in L^{2}$. Then:

(a) $A$ and $H$ are self-adjoint with domain $D(A)=W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C)$,
and $H=cA$ and $H_{0}=cA_{0}$ hold as operator identities on that common domain;

(b) for every Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb R$,
$$E_{H}(cB)=E_{A}(B),\qquad E_{H_{0}}(cB)=E_{A_{0}}(B);$$
consequently $\mu^{H}_{\psi}(cB)=\mu^{A}_{\psi}(B)$ for every $\psi$ and every
Borel $B$, and $\sigma(H)=c\,\sigma(A)$, $\sigma(H_{0})=c\,\sigma(A_{0})$;

(c) for every $t\in\mathbb R$, with $\tau:=\hbar t/(2m)=\frac{tc}{\hbar}$,
$$e^{-itH/\hbar}=e^{-i\tau A},\qquad e^{-itH_{0}/\hbar}=e^{-i\tau A_{0}},$$
where the exponentials are those of
[[lem-self-adjoint-operator-generates-a-strongly-continuous-unitary-group]];

$\tau(t):=\hbar t/(2m)$. For every $\psi\in L^{2}$ the strong limit
$\lim_{t\to\pm\infty}F(\tau(t))\psi$ exists if and only if
$\lim_{\tau\to\pm\infty}F(\tau)\psi$ exists, and then the two limits are equal;

$$\operatorname*{s-lim}_{t\to\pm\infty}e^{itH/\hbar}e^{-itH_{0}/\hbar} =\operatorname*{s-lim}_{\tau\to\pm\infty}e^{i\tau A}e^{-i\tau A_{0}}$$

then they are equal;

with eigenvalue $\lambda/c$.

no physical interpretation, no scattering limit and no cross section is
asserted.

If $K_\varepsilon\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ satisfy
$$\int K_\varepsilon=1,\qquad M:=\sup_{\varepsilon>0}\|K_\varepsilon\|_1<\infty,\qquad \int_{|y|\ge\delta}|K_\varepsilon(y)|\,dy\longrightarrow0\quad(\delta>0),$$
then $K_\varepsilon*f\to f$ in $L^p$ for $p<\infty$, and uniformly for $f\in C_0(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. For fixed $K\in L^1$, $K*f\in C_0$ when $f\in C_0$. These assertions allow complex and sign-changing kernels. In particular $K_\varepsilon(x)=\varepsilon^{-n}K(x/\varepsilon)$ is such an approximate identity whenever $K\in L^1$ and $\int K=1$.

If $\rho\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb R)$ has mass one, $\rho_\varepsilon(x)=\varepsilon^{-n}\rho(x/\varepsilon)$, and $f$ is complex locally integrable, then $\rho_\varepsilon*f$ is smooth and
$$\partial^\alpha(\rho_\varepsilon*f)=(\partial^\alpha\rho_\varepsilon)*f.$$
A compactly supported input gives a compactly supported output. No general $L^\infty$ translation-continuity or approximate-identity convergence is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $m,\hbar>0$, put
$c:=2\pi^{2}\hbar^{2}/m$, and let $H_{0}$ be the free operator of
[[thm-nrqm-composites-real-multipliers-and-free-bounded-potential-operators]]
clause (b) with $d=3$, this $c$ and $b=0$:
$$H_{0}:=\mathcal F_{2}^{*}M_{c|\xi|^{2}}\mathcal F_{2},\qquad D(H_{0}):=\bigl\{f\in L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C):|\xi|^{2}\mathcal F_{2}f\in L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C)\bigr\},$$
where $\mathcal F_{2}$ is the unitary Plancherel transform of that theorem.
Let $D^{2}_{j}$ denote the second weak partial derivative in the $j$-th
coordinate, defined componentwise on the locally integrable classes of
$\mathbb R^{3}$ ([[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]),
write $\Delta_{w}:=D^{2}_{1}+D^{2}_{2}+D^{2}_{3}$ for the weak Laplacian
(defined on the classes whose three second weak partial derivatives lie in
$L^{2}$), and let $W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C)$ be the Sobolev space
([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]). Then:

(a) $D(H_{0})=W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C)$ as sets and
$$H_{0}f=-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}\,\Delta_{w}f\qquad\text{for every }f\in D(H_{0});$$
equivalently, $\mathcal F_{2}(H_{0}f)(\xi)=c|\xi|^{2}\mathcal F_{2}f(\xi)$ and
$\mathcal F_{2}\bigl(-\tfrac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}\Delta_{w}f\bigr)(\xi)=c|\xi|^{2}\mathcal F_{2}f(\xi)$
for almost every $\xi$, and the two $L^{2}$ classes agree.

(b) For every real bounded measurable $V:\mathbb R^{3}\to\mathbb R$, the
operator $H_{0}+M_{V}$ of clause (c) of the cited theorem, with domain
$D(H_{0})$, coincides with the operator $f\mapsto-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}\Delta_{w}f+Vf$
on the same domain; in particular, for $E\in\mathbb R$ and
$\psi\in W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C)$ the eigenvalue equation
$(H_{0}+M_{V})\psi=E\psi$ is equivalent to the weak equation
$-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}\Delta_{w}\psi+V\psi=E\psi$ elementwise in
$L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C)$.

The statement identifies operators on the same domain; it asserts neither
smoothness of the classes in $W^{2,2}$ nor any physical interpretation.

derivations.claim: Put $W_*(y)=V(L_*y)/E_*=W_{*,2}(y)+W_{*,\mathrm b}(y)$. Lebesgue dilation gives $\|W_{*,2}\|_2=E_*^{-1}L_*^{-3/2}\|V_2\|_2$ and $\|W_{*,\mathrm b}\|_\infty=E_*^{-1}\|V_{\mathrm b}\|_\infty$. Thus these parts are real $L^2$ and bounded functions respectively. In [F2] use the dimensionless variable $y$ in place of its abstract variable $x$, $V_0=W_*$ and $A_{0,*}=-\Delta_y^{\mathrm{weak}}$. The full hypothesis is exactly $h_*(r)<\infty$ for every $r$ with $h_*\in L^1$, so [F2] gives self-adjoint $A_*$ on $H^2_y$, isometric wave operators $\Omega_{\pm,*}$, $H_{\mathrm{sc}}(A_*)=0$, equal ranges $H_{\mathrm{ac}}(A_*)=H_{\mathrm c}(A_*)$ and unitary $S_*$.

[Failure of the general Coulomb resolvent-tail condition] For the pure Coulomb reduced potential put $W_{*,C}=-\gamma_*/|y|$, $\gamma_*=\kappa/(E_*L_*)>0$. All radii in this argument are dimensionless. Fix by [F4] a nonzero real $\phi\in C_c^\infty(B_R)$, and for $r>R$ set $\phi_r(y)=\phi(y-2r e_1)$ and $f_r=(A_{0,*}-i)\phi_r$. Both are supported outside the radius-$r$ ball, since $2r-R>r$; derivatives do not enlarge support. The free derivative action and translation isometry give $\|\phi_r\|_2=\|\phi\|_2>0$ and $\|f_r\|_2=\|(A_{0,*}-i)\phi\|_2=:c_f>0$. Positivity and self-adjointness of $A_{0,*}$ ensure its resolvent at $i$ exists, and $(A_{0,*}-i)^{-1}\mathbf1_{\{|y|\ge r\}}f_r=\phi_r$. If the Coulomb resolvent-tail operator is not bounded at some radius it already fails the class; otherwise its operator norm obeys $h_{*,C}(r)\ge\frac{\|M_{W_{*,C}}\phi_r\|_2}{\|f_r\|_2}\ge\frac{\gamma_*\|\phi\|_2}{c_f(2r+R)}.$ The last bound uses $|y|\le2r+R$ on that support. The positive lower bound has divergent integral over $r>R$, so $h_{*,C}\notin L^1([0,\infty))$. Thus pure Coulomb fails the general class as well, proving the general-class exclusion in (d) without any zero-energy hypothesis.

By [F1], $H=D_*^*E_*A_*D_*$ is self-adjoint on $W^{2,2}_x$. For $\tau=t/T_*$ the physical comparison is $D_*^*e^{i\tau A_*}e^{-i\tau A_{0,*}}D_*$. Since $T_*>0$, each physical infinite-time limit exists and equals $D_*^*\Omega_{\pm,*}D_*$. These are isometries, their ranges are the conjugated spectral subspaces $H_{\mathrm{ac}}(H)=H_{\mathrm c}(H)$ and $H_{\mathrm{sc}}(H)=0$. This proves (a).
By [F3] and step 2.1, $S=D_*^*S_*D_*$, which is unitary since $S_*$ and $D_*$ are unitary. This proves (b).

For the physical decay form in (c), set $W_{*,\mathrm{loc}}(y)=V_{\mathrm{loc}}(L_*y)/E_*$ and $W_{*,\mathrm{tail}}(y)=V_{\mathrm{tail}}(L_*y)/E_*$. The local part has norm $E_*^{-1}L_*^{-3/2}\|V_{\mathrm{loc}}\|_2$ and support radius divided by $L_*$. The tail satisfies $|W_{*,\mathrm{tail}}(y)|\le(C/E_*)(1+|y|)^{-1-\delta}$. Thus [F2]'s full sufficient-decay result supplies the integrable resolvent-input tail and all conclusions for $A_*$; step 2.1 and step 3.1 transfer them to the physical operators. This proves (c) without assuming the resolvent estimate for this example.

For $V(x)=-\kappa/|x|$ with $\kappa>0$ and any split $V=V_{\mathrm{loc}}+V_{\mathrm{tail}}$ into a compactly supported part and the remainder, the remainder equals $-\kappa/|x|$ for all sufficiently large $|x|$, so for every $\delta>0$ the quotient $(1+|x|/L_*)^{1+\delta}|V_{\mathrm{tail}}(x)|=\kappa(1+|x|/L_*)^{1+\delta}/|x|$ tends to $+\infty$ as $|x|\to\infty$; hence no constant $C$ satisfies the sufficient decay bound of [F2]'s final paragraph, and the explicit form of (c) does not cover the Coulomb potential. This proves the sufficient-decay exclusion in (d).
