The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(-x)=-\sin x,\qquad\cos(-x)=\cos x,\qquad\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.$$
Consequently $|\sin x|\le1$ and $|\cos x|\le1$.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, and suppose $f$ has derivatives through order $n+1$ on the closed interval between $a$ and $x$, with the usual endpoint continuity. If $|f^{(n+1)}(t)|\le M$ throughout that interval, then
$$|R_{n,a}f(x)|\le \frac{M}{\iota((n+1)!)}|x-a|^{n+1}.$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-continuity-real]]), and let $y \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$f(a) \le y \le f(b) \qquad \text{or} \qquad f(b) \le y \le f(a) .$$

Then there is $c \in [a,b]$ with $f(c) = y$.

**The construction is canonical, so no choice principle is used.** The bisection
below tests the left half first and takes the right half only when the left one
has been ruled out, so the passage from one interval to the next is a *function*
of that interval, and [[thm-recursion]] applies with nothing selected. This is
the same discipline the library uses wherever a sequence is built one term at a
time.

**Completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ is what does the work.** The bisection produces a
nested sequence of closed bounded intervals whose lengths tend to $0$, and it is
[[thm-nested-interval-property]] — hence the least-upper-bound property — that
supplies the point. Over an ordered field that is not complete the theorem
fails; the witness for that, stated for an arbitrary ordered field and worked
over $\mathbb{Q}$, is
[[cex-evt-and-ivt-fail-over-a-non-complete-field]], which states its own
$\varepsilon$-$\delta$ continuity inline and is not an instance of this page's
definition.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n \ge 1$,
let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the
set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$
is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$, and for every Borel measurable
$f : \mathbb R^n \to [0,\infty]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$
Moreover, $\sigma$ is the unique Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ with this
property.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$S^2:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:|x|=1\}$ and let $\sigma$ be the polar surface measure on $S^2$ of
[[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]], a finite Borel measure ([[def-measure]],
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Let

$$\Phi:(0,\pi)\times(0,2\pi)\to S^2,\qquad \Phi(\theta,\varphi):=(\sin\theta\cos\varphi,\ \sin\theta\sin\varphi,\ \cos\theta),$$

and let $H:=\{(x,y,0)\in\mathbb R^3:x\ge0\}$ denote the closed half-plane, a Lebesgue-null Borel set
([[thm-affine-hyperplanes-and-proper-subspaces-of-rn-are-lebesgue-null]]). Then:

(a) for every Borel function $F:S^2\to[0,+\infty]$,
$$\int_{S^2}F\,d\sigma=\int_{(0,\pi)\times(0,2\pi)}F\bigl(\Phi(\theta,\varphi)\bigr)\,\sin\theta\ d(\theta,\varphi),$$
the right-hand integral being the Lebesgue integral over the open rectangle;

(b) $\sigma(S^2)=4\pi$;

(c) the identity of (a) holds with $F\in L^1(S^2,\sigma;\mathbb C)$ in the sense that $F\circ\Phi$ is Lebesgue
integrable on the rectangle against $\sin\theta\,d(\theta,\varphi)$ and the two integrals agree (real and
imaginary parts, positive and negative parts).

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

**(a) Framework data.** Adopt the state and composition postulate P1, the
observable and probability postulate P2, the autonomous-dynamics postulate P4,
the kinematics and massive-particle model postulate P5, the identical-particle
and spin postulate P6, and the preparation and apparatus discipline P7
([[post-nrqm-framework-state-and-composition]],
[[post-nrqm-framework-observable-and-probability]],
[[post-nrqm-framework-autonomous-dynamics]],
[[post-nrqm-framework-nonrelativistic-kinematics-and-massive-particle]],
[[post-nrqm-framework-identical-particles-and-spin]],
[[post-nrqm-framework-preparation-and-apparatus]]). Fix a mass parameter
$m>0$ and a spin label $s=0$, so that the framework's one-particle model
[[def-nrqm-kinematics-framework-massive-spin-s-model]] reads its state space as
$H_{0}=L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C)$ with the pairing linear in the first
argument, its componentwise position family $Q_{1},Q_{2},Q_{3}$, its
componentwise momentum family $P_{1},P_{2},P_{3}$ and the action constant
$\hbar>0$; the spin-zero internal factor carries the trivial representation of
P6. Units are those of [[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]]: position
is read in metres, momentum in $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$, energy and potential
energy in joules, and $\hbar$ in $\mathrm{J\,s}$. Assume the Axiom of
Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice as the choice hypotheses of the cited
mathematical suppliers ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

Choose a reference length $L_*>0$ in metres and put
$$y=x/L_*,\qquad E_*:=\frac{\hbar^2}{2mL_*^2},\qquad T_*:=\hbar/E_*.$$
Here $y$ is dimensionless, $E_*$ is in joules and $T_*$ in seconds.
The unitary coordinate dilation from physical-coordinate $L^2_x$ to
$L^2_y$ is $(D_*f)(y)=L_*^{3/2}f(L_*y)$, with inverse
$(D_*^*g)(x)=L_*^{-3/2}g(x/L_*)$. Lebesgue dilation
([[thm-lebesgue-measure-under-dilations-and-reflections]]) gives its norm
identity, first for simple functions and then by nonnegative approximation.
This convention makes all coordinates and spectral shifts in the tail
criterion below dimensionless; physical stationary equations retain $x$.

**(b) The declared scattering model and its potential classes.** As an
additional model assumption of the pair, adopt the **short-range scattering
model**. Its declared state space is $H_{0}=L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C)$ of
clause (a), with the position and momentum families of that clause. A
**declared short-range potential** of the model is a real-valued measurable
function $V:\mathbb R^{3}\to\mathbb R$ satisfying either

1. *(compact-support class)* $V$ is bounded, $\|V\|_{\infty}<\infty$, and
   $V=0$ almost everywhere outside some ball
   $B_{\mathrm{supp}}:=\{x:|x|\le R_{\mathrm{supp}}\}$ with
   $R_{\mathrm{supp}}<\infty$; or
2. *(resolvent-tail class)* $V=V_{2}+V_{\mathrm b}$ with real
   $V_{2}\in L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3})$ and real bounded $V_{\mathrm b}$, and, with
   the dimensionless reduced potential
   $W_*(y):=V(L_*y)/E_*=W_{*,2}(y)+W_{*,\mathrm b}(y)$ and
   $A_{0,*}:=-\Delta_y^{\mathrm{weak}}$ on $W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^3_y)$,
   the function
$$h_*(r):=\bigl\|M_{W_*}(A_{0,*}-iI)^{-1}\mathbf 1_{\{|y|\ge r\}}\bigr\|,\qquad r\ge0,$$
   is finite for every dimensionless $r$ and belongs to $L^1([0,\infty),dr)$.
   Equivalently the physical-coordinate operator is
   $M_V(H^{\mathrm{free}}-iE_*I)^{-1}\mathbf1_{\{|x|\ge L_*r\}}$:
   conjugation by $D_*$ gives exactly the displayed operator. Thus physical
   cutoffs have radius $L_*r$, and integration in physical radius $R$ gives
   $\int_0^\infty h_*(R/L_*)\,dR=L_*\int_0^\infty h_*(r)\,dr$.
   The reference length is fixed as part of this unit convention.

The function $V$ is read as a potential energy in joules; the model asserts no
derivation of $V$ from P5 or from any force law, and an assignment of a
concrete target to $V$ is a tested identification in the sense of clause (iii)
of P7 carrying the corresponding uncertainty. The pure Coulomb potential
$V(x)=-\kappa/|x|$, $\kappa>0$, is **not** in either class: it is a declared
long-range model with its own definition and comparison construction
on this page.

**(c) Assigned energy observables.** Let $\mathcal F_{2}$ be the unitary
Plancherel transform of
[[thm-nrqm-composites-real-multipliers-and-free-bounded-potential-operators]]
clause (b), $c:=2\pi^{2}\hbar^{2}/m$, and let
$$H^{\mathrm{free}}:=\mathcal F_{2}^{*}M_{c|\xi|^{2}}\mathcal F_{2},\qquad D(H^{\mathrm{free}}):=\bigl\{f\in H_{0}:|\xi|^{2}\mathcal F_{2}f\in H_{0}\bigr\}$$
be the free operator of that clause with $d=3$ and $b=0$; by
[[lem-nrqm-central-free-operator-differential-identification]] its domain is
the Sobolev space $W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C)$
([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]) and
$H^{\mathrm{free}}f=-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}\Delta_{w}f$ with $\Delta_{w}$ the
weak Laplacian ([[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]).
For equations in physical coordinates write $A_{0,x}:=-\Delta_x^{\mathrm{weak}}$
and $W_x(x):=2mV(x)/\hbar^2$, so
$H^{\mathrm{free}}=(\hbar^2/2m)A_{0,x}$. Both $A_{0,x}$ and $W_x$
have inverse-square-length units; this energy division alone is not a
spatial nondimensionalization. Stationary items may abbreviate $W_x$ as $W$
(or its central radial profile as $w$), keeping physical $k$ and $r$.
The dimensionless operators instead satisfy
$$D_*H^{\mathrm{free}}D_*^*=E_*A_{0,*},\qquad D_*HD_*^*=E_*(A_{0,*}+M_{W_*}),\qquad W_*(y)=L_*^2W_x(L_*y).$$
Indeed testing the weak derivative definition after $x=L_*y$ gives
$\partial_y^\alpha D_*f=L_*^{|\alpha|}D_*(\partial_x^\alpha f)$ for
$|\alpha|\le2$; applying the inverse dilation gives the converse, so $D_*$
maps the physical Sobolev domain onto the dimensionless one. Multiplication
transforms by direct substitution, proving both operator identities on their
exact domains. The subscript $w$ in $\Delta_w$ above denotes weak derivatives,
not a coordinate or a unit convention.
With $M_V$ the maximal multiplication operator, $D(M_V)=\{f\in L^2:Vf\in L^2\}$ (bounded and everywhere defined in the compact-support class), the **assigned energy observables** of the model with declared
potential $V$ are the free operator $H^{\mathrm{free}}$ and the interacting
operator
$$H:=H^{\mathrm{free}}+M_{V},\qquad D(H):=D(H^{\mathrm{free}}).$$
The declared energy unit is the joule. For the compact-support class,
clause (c) of the cited theorem makes $H$ self-adjoint on $D(H)$ and bounded
below by $-\|V\|_{\infty}$. For the resolvent-tail class,
[[thm-nrqm-controlled-dynamics-resolvent-tail-short-range-completeness]]
(Statement and proof step 1.1) applies to $W_*=W_{*,2}+W_{*,\mathrm b}$:
$\|W_{*,2}\|_2=E_*^{-1}L_*^{-3/2}\|V_2\|_2<\infty$,
$\|W_{*,\mathrm b}\|_\infty=E_*^{-1}\|V_{\mathrm b}\|_\infty<\infty$,
and its tail hypothesis is exactly clause (b)2. That supplier proves
$H^2_y\subseteq D(M_{W_*})$ and self-adjointness of
$A_{0,*}+M_{W_*}$ on $H^2_y=W^{2,2}_y$. The displayed unitary dilation and
positive scaling therefore give $D(H^{\mathrm{free}})\subseteq D(M_V)$
and self-adjointness of $H$ on precisely $W^{2,2}_x$, without assuming
that $V_2$ is bounded. The
model adopts $(H^{\mathrm{free}},\mathrm J)$ and $(H,\mathrm J)$ as assigned
sharp observables in the sense of
[[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]] clause (a), and
reads their flows by [[def-nrqm-autonomous-dynamics-framework-evolution]]
with $U_{\mathrm{free}}(t)=e^{-itH^{\mathrm{free}}/\hbar}$ and
$U(t)=e^{-itH/\hbar}$.

**(d) Short-range scattering vocabulary.** For a declared short-range
potential $V$ the model declares the **free asymptotic comparison** to be the
pair of strong limits
$$\Omega_{\pm}:=\operatorname*{s-lim}_{t\to\pm\infty}e^{itH/\hbar}e^{-itH^{\mathrm{free}}/\hbar},$$
which are declared **wave operators** of the model when both limits exist, and
declares the **scattering operator** $S:=\Omega_{+}^{*}\Omega_{-}$ when both
exist and $\Omega_{\pm}$ are isometries. The model says that the pair is
**asymptotically complete** for this $V$ when the two ranges agree with the
subspace
$$H_{\mathrm{ac}}(H):=\{\psi\in H_{0}:\mu^{H}_{\psi}\ll\lambda\},$$
where $\mu^{H}_{\psi}(B):=\langle E_{H}(B)\psi,\psi\rangle$ is the scalar
spectral measure of the projection valued measure $E_{H}$ of the self-adjoint
operator $H$, and with
$$H_{\mathrm c}(H):=H_{\mathrm{pp}}(H)^{\perp},\qquad H_{\mathrm{pp}}(H):=\overline{\operatorname{span}}\{\psi\ne0:H\psi=\lambda\psi\ \text{for some }\lambda\in\mathbb R\};$$
here $H_{\mathrm{pp}}(H)$ is the closed linear span of the eigenvectors of $H$.
An **asymptotic free state** of a vector $\psi\in H_{0}$ is a vector
$\psi_{\mathrm{in}}$ such that
$\bigl\|e^{-itH/\hbar}\psi-e^{-itH^{\mathrm{free}}/\hbar}\psi_{\mathrm{in}}\bigr\|\to0$
as $t\to-\infty$; the model reads this limit relation through the
wave-operator identity $\psi=\Omega_{-}\psi_{\mathrm{in}}$ only when the wave
operator exists. These
are declarations of the model under P4; they construct no preparation,
detector or measured count, and no definition of a cross section appears here.

**(e) Status and scope.** Clause (a) adopts P1, P2, P4, P5, P6 and P7 and
fixes the pair's spin-zero one-particle data, mass, action constant and choice
hypotheses. Clause (b) further adopts the compact-support and resolvent-tail
potential classes as **additional pair-level model assumptions**; neither
class follows from those postulates or from the cited mathematical results.
Clause (c) declares the assigned energy operators and their common domain;
the cited mathematics establishes self-adjointness where stated, including
the resolvent-tail case supplied by the cited mathematical theorem. Clause (d) declares the
comparison and spectral vocabulary without asserting that the limits exist
or are complete. No identification of $m$, $\hbar$ or $V$ with measured data
is asserted. Existence of the limits, completeness of the ranges and every
cross section are separate results of the pair.

derivations.claim: For $r<a$ the reduced equation is $u_0''=-K^2u_0$, so its nonzero real regular solution is $u_0(r)=A\sin(Kr)$, $A\ne0$, with $u_0(0)=0$; the normalization in [F1] corresponds to $A=1/K$. For $r>a$ a nonzero real solution has the form $B\sin(kr+\delta_0)$ with real $B\ne0$. The regular solution and its derivative are absolutely continuous locally through the bounded step potential; integrating the radial equation across $a$ gives no jump of $u_0'$ or $u_0$. Thus $A\sin(Ka)=B\sin(ka+\delta_0)$ and $AK\cos(Ka)=Bk\cos(ka+\delta_0)$.

Put $X:=K\cos(Ka)$, $Y:=k\sin(Ka)$ and $z:=X+iY$. Since $k,K>0$ and sine and cosine cannot both vanish, $X^2+Y^2>0$. With $\theta:=ka+\delta_0$, the matching equations give $Bk\cos\theta=AX$, $Bk\sin\theta=AY$, hence $e^{2i\theta}=z/\overline z$ regardless of the real sign of $A/B$. Consequently $S_0(k)=e^{-2ika}\,(K\cos(Ka)+ik\sin(Ka))/(K\cos(Ka)-ik\sin(Ka))$ and $\delta_0=\arg z-ka$ modulo $\pi$, with a nonzero denominator for every positive energy and depth. This is also the actual Wronskian convention of [F1], since outside the well $W(u_0,e^{ikr})=-Bk e^{-i\delta_0}$. Where $\cos(Ka)\ne0$, the equivalent local formula is $\tan(ka+\delta_0)=(k/K)\tan(Ka)$; the complex formula remains valid when either matching value vanishes.

Fix $U>0$ and put $\gamma:=\sqrt{2mU}/\hbar$, so $K=\sqrt{\gamma^2+k^2}$ and $K-\gamma=k^2/(K+\gamma)=O(k^2)$. If $\cos(\gamma a)\ne0$, choose the representative of $\theta$ tending to zero modulo $\pi$. The tangent is smooth near $\gamma a$, so $\tan\theta=(k/K)\tan(Ka)=k\tan(\gamma a)/\gamma+O(k^3)$. By [F2], $\tan\theta=\theta+O(\theta^3)$ near zero; first $\theta=O(k)$ and then $\theta=k\tan(\gamma a)/\gamma+O(k^3)$. Hence $\delta_0=-k a_{\mathrm{eff}}+O(k^3)$ modulo $\pi$, where $a_{\mathrm{eff}}:=a-\tan(\gamma a)/\gamma$, and [F1] gives $\sigma_0\to4\pi a_{\mathrm{eff}}^2$. The expansion uses locally bounded derivatives only where $\cos(\gamma a)\ne0$.

At an exact threshold $\gamma a=\alpha_n:=(n+\tfrac12)\pi$, $n\ge0$, write $s_n:=\sin\alpha_n=(-1)^n$. The identity for $K-\gamma$ and [F2] give $K-\gamma=k^2/(2\gamma)+O(k^4)$, $X=K\cos(Ka)=-s_n a k^2/2+O(k^4)$ and $Y=k\sin(Ka)=s_n k+O(k^5)$. Thus $X/Y=-ak/2+O(k^3)$ and the angle of $X+iY$ tends to $\pi/2$ modulo $\pi$. Writing $\theta=\pi/2+\varepsilon$ modulo $\pi$, $\cot\theta=-\varepsilon+O(\varepsilon^3)$ gives $\varepsilon=ak/2+O(k^3)$, so $\delta_0=\pi/2-ak/2+O(k^3)$ modulo $\pi$. Therefore $k^2\sigma_0=4\pi\sin^2\delta_0\to4\pi$; the finite-scattering-length formula of step 3.1 does not apply at this depth. At zero energy the regular reduced solution is proportional to $\sin(\gamma r)$ inside and to the nonzero constant $s_n$ outside, with matching derivative zero at $a$. Its spatial form is proportional to $1/r$ outside and is not square integrable by [F3]; this is the zero-energy s-wave resonance meant here.

In the finite-length branch, as $\gamma a\uparrow\alpha_n$ from below, $\tan(\gamma a)\to+\infty$ and $a_{\mathrm{eff}}\to-\infty$; from above $a_{\mathrm{eff}}\to+\infty$. Thus the iterated low-energy reading $4\pi a_{\mathrm{eff}}^2$ diverges on either approach, while the exact-threshold law is step 4.1. Along nonresonant depth regimes with $\tan(\gamma a)/\gamma\to0$, $a_{\mathrm{eff}}\to a$ and the iterated low-energy reading tends to $4\pi a^2$, four times the geometric area $\pi a^2$. In particular at $\gamma a=n\pi$, $n\ge1$, $a_{\mathrm{eff}}=a$ and $\delta_0=-ka+O(k^3)$; the interior node tends to the boundary. This comparison holds along the stated depth regimes, rather than for every sequence of large depths.

The bound-state interpretation has a separate negative-energy proof. Write $g:=\gamma a$. For $\alpha_n<g<(n+1)\pi$, define $f_g(x):=x\cot x+\sqrt{g^2-x^2}$ on $[\alpha_n,g]$. It is continuous, $f_g(\alpha_n)=\sqrt{g^2-\alpha_n^2}>0$ and $f_g(g)=g\cot g<0$; [F2] gives a root $x_g\in(\alpha_n,g)$. On that open interval $f_g'=\cot x-x\csc^2x-x/\sqrt{g^2-x^2}<0$, so the root is unique. Put $q:=x_g/a$, $\kappa:=\sqrt{g^2-x_g^2}/a>0$ and $u(r):=\sin(qr)$ for $r\le a$, $u(r):=\sin(qa)e^{-\kappa(r-a)}$ for $r\ge a$. Then $q^2+\kappa^2=\gamma^2$ and $q\cot(qa)=-\kappa$, so both $u$ and $u'$ match at $a$. The spatial function $\psi(x):=u(|x|)/|x|$, with value $q$ at zero, is nonzero and square integrable by [F3]; it is smooth near zero, decays exponentially at infinity and is piecewise smooth with matching first derivatives at $a$. Its weak derivatives through order two are square integrable, with no boundary delta term, hence $\psi\in W^{2,2}$. The radial identity $\Delta(u(r)/r)=u''(r)/r$ for $r>0$ gives $H\psi=-c\kappa^2\psi$, $c=\hbar^2/(2m)$, so normalization produces a genuine s-wave bound eigenvector. As $g\downarrow\alpha_n$, $0<\kappa a\le\sqrt{g^2-\alpha_n^2}\to0$, while for $g\le\alpha_n$ there is no matching root in this branch $x>\alpha_n$ with $x\le g$. Thus a new negative-energy s-wave branch appears just above each stated threshold, whose endpoint is the non-square-integrable zero-energy resonance in step 4.1; no assertion about other angular channels or the full bound-state count is needed.

For the free consistency case $U=0$, $K=k$ and step 2.1 gives $S_0=e^{-2ika}(\cos ka+i\sin ka)/(\cos ka-i\sin ka)=1$, so $\delta_0=0$ modulo $\pi$ at every positive energy, including zeros of sine or cosine. At any positive-depth energy with $Ka=n\pi$, $n\ge1$, one has $Y=0$ and $X\ne0$, hence $S_0=e^{-2ika}$ and $\delta_0=-ka$ modulo $\pi$: this is exactly the exterior phase for the vanishing radial boundary condition of a hard sphere at that energy. If $\cos(Ka)=0$, the same formula gives $S_0=-e^{-2ika}$ and $\delta_0=\pi/2-ka$ modulo $\pi$. These checks complete the full positive-energy, zero-depth and matching-node cases together with the two low-energy branches above.

derivations.claim: Since $E_r>0$, the theorem can be evaluated at the physical energy $E_r$, giving $\sin^2\delta_0(E_r)=L(E_r)=1$ and $\sigma_0(E_r)=4\pi/k_r^2=4\pi\hbar^2/(2mE_r)$ in $\mathrm{m^2}$. The real-axis factor has $L(E_r\pm\Gamma/2)=1/2$. The upper point is always positive; the lower point is positive exactly if $\Gamma<2E_r$, equals the excluded boundary $0$ if $\Gamma=2E_r$, and is negative if $\Gamma>2E_r$. Only positive points have physical phase and cross-section readings.

For every physical $E>0$, with $x:=E-E_r$ and $y:=\Gamma/2>0$, dividing by the positive resonance-centre value yields $\sigma_0(E)/\sigma_0(E_r)=(k_r/k(E))^2 y^2/(x^2+y^2)=(E_r/E)L(E)$. At the always-positive upper point the ratio is $E_r/(2(E_r+y))$; at the lower point it is $E_r/(2(E_r-y))$ only when $E_r-y>0$. If that lower point is zero or negative, the real-axis identity $L(E_r-y)=1/2$ is still valid but no physical ratio is evaluated there. The factor $E_r/E$ is energy dependent and need not vary slowly for arbitrary $\Gamma$.

Take the declared parameters $E_{r}=4\,\Gamma$ (both in joules). Then at $E=E_{r}+\Gamma/2=(9/2)\Gamma$ the Lorentzian factor is $1/2$ and the ratio of step 2.1 is $(4/(9/2))(1/2)=4/9$; at $E=(7/2)\Gamma$ the factor is again $1/2$ and the ratio is $(4/(7/2))(1/2)=4/7$. The first value is strictly below $1/2$ and the second strictly above, so this is the explicit asymmetry produced by the $1/E$ factor, so these factor half-height locations are not the locations where $\sigma_0(E)=\sigma_0(E_r)/2$; no maximum of $\sigma_0$ is used in this comparison.

On the full real axis, $L$ reaches $1$ at $E_r$ and $1/2$ exactly at $E_r\pm\Gamma/2$, so its full width at half maximum is $\Gamma$. On the positive physical axis both half-height locations are present exactly when $\Gamma<2E_r$; for $\Gamma\ge2E_r$ the lower location is excluded. derivations.claim: By the Born theorem, $f_{B}(\Omega)=-\frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{B_{R}}e^{i\mathbf q_{\mathrm{tr}}\cdot y}W(y)\,dy$ with $W=V_{0}2m/\hbar^{2}$ constant on $B_{R}$; in polar coordinates the ball integral is $\int_{B_{R}}e^{iq\cdot y}dy=2\pi\int_{0}^{R}\int_{-1}^{1}e^{iqrs}r^{2}\,ds\,dr=4\pi\bigl(\sin(qR)-qR\cos(qR)\bigr)/q^{3}$ for $q=q_{\mathrm{tr}}>0$, and equals $4\pi R^{3}/3$ at $q=0$ by continuity. [given, algebra]

The kernel $G_{k}(x-y)W(y)$ on $B_{R}\times B_{R}$ has squared Hilbert-Schmidt norm $\int_{B_{R}}\int_{B_{R}}|G_{k}(x-y)W(y)|^{2}dx\,dy=\frac{|V_{0}|^{2}(2m/\hbar^{2})^{2}}{16\pi^{2}}\int_{B_{R}}\int_{B_{R}}|x-y|^{-2}dx\,dy$; for each $y$ the inner integral over $x\in B_{R}$ is at most the integral over the ball of radius $2R$ around $y$, which is $8\pi R$. Hence $\|K_{k}\|\le\|K_{k}\|_{\mathrm{HS}}\le\frac{2m|V_{0}|}{\hbar^{2}}R^{2}\sqrt{2/3}=:q_{\mathrm{HS}}$. [given, algebra]

Therefore $f_{B}(\Omega)=-\frac{2mV_{0}}{\hbar^{2}}\cdot\frac{\sin(q_{\mathrm{tr}}R)-q_{\mathrm{tr}}R\cos(q_{\mathrm{tr}}R)}{q_{\mathrm{tr}}^{3}}$ for $q_{\mathrm{tr}}>0$, with the forward value $f_{B}(\theta=0)=-\frac{2mV_{0}}{\hbar^{2}}\frac{R^{3}}{3}$; the amplitude has the dimension of length, since $2mV_{0}/\hbar^{2}$ is in $\mathrm{m^{-2}}$ and the bracket in $\mathrm{m^{3}}$. [step 1.1, algebra]

Consequently, if $\frac{2m|V_{0}|}{\hbar^{2}}R^{2}\sqrt{2/3}<1$, then $q=\|K_{k}\|\le q_{\mathrm{HS}}<1$ and the controlled Born estimate of the theorem applies; since $t\mapsto t/(1-t)$ is increasing on $[0,1)$ and $\|e_{\mathrm{inc}}\|_{L^{2}(B_{R})}=|B_{R}|^{1/2}$, the uniform error bound is at most $|f_{k}(\Omega)-f_{B}(\Omega)|\le\frac{\|W\|_{\infty}|B_{R}|}{4\pi}\frac{q_{\mathrm{HS}}}{1-q_{\mathrm{HS}}}=\frac{2m|V_{0}|}{\hbar^{2}}\frac{R^{3}}{3}\frac{q_{\mathrm{HS}}}{1-q_{\mathrm{HS}}}$ in metres; this is an explicit condition on the declared strength, radius, mass and action constant, verified here without any numerical value of the constants. [step 1.2, given, algebra]

Under the same condition the beam model reads $d\sigma/d\Omega(0)=|f_{k}(0)|^{2}$, and the theorem controls the difference from $|f_{B}(0)|^{2}$ through the bound of 2.2; the pair asserts the display $|f_{B}(0)|^{2}=\bigl(\frac{2mV_{0}}{\hbar^{2}}\bigr)^{2}\frac{R^{6}}{9}$ as the Born forward reading, read in $\mathrm{m^{2}\,sr^{-1}}$, and no measured value. citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n \ge 1$,
let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the
set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$
is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$, and for every Borel measurable
$f : \mathbb R^n \to [0,\infty]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$
Moreover, $\sigma$ is the unique Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ with this
property.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$S^2:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:|x|=1\}$ and let $\sigma$ be the polar surface measure on $S^2$ of
[[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]], a finite Borel measure ([[def-measure]],
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Let

$$\Phi:(0,\pi)\times(0,2\pi)\to S^2,\qquad \Phi(\theta,\varphi):=(\sin\theta\cos\varphi,\ \sin\theta\sin\varphi,\ \cos\theta),$$

and let $H:=\{(x,y,0)\in\mathbb R^3:x\ge0\}$ denote the closed half-plane, a Lebesgue-null Borel set
([[thm-affine-hyperplanes-and-proper-subspaces-of-rn-are-lebesgue-null]]). Then:

(a) for every Borel function $F:S^2\to[0,+\infty]$,
$$\int_{S^2}F\,d\sigma=\int_{(0,\pi)\times(0,2\pi)}F\bigl(\Phi(\theta,\varphi)\bigr)\,\sin\theta\ d(\theta,\varphi),$$
the right-hand integral being the Lebesgue integral over the open rectangle;

(b) $\sigma(S^2)=4\pi$;

(c) the identity of (a) holds with $F\in L^1(S^2,\sigma;\mathbb C)$ in the sense that $F\circ\Phi$ is Lebesgue
integrable on the rectangle against $\sin\theta\,d(\theta,\varphi)$ and the two integrals agree (real and
imaginary parts, positive and negative parts).

derivations.claim: Put $V_{\mathrm{loc}}:=V_{g,\mu}\mathbf1_{\{|x|<L_*\}}$ and $V_{\mathrm{tail}}:=V_{g,\mu}\mathbf1_{\{|x|\ge L_*\}}$. The local part is supported in the closed radius-$L_*$ ball, and polar integration gives $\int|V_{\mathrm{loc}}|^2dx=4\pi g^2\int_0^{L_*}e^{-2\mu r}dr \le4\pi g^2L_*<\infty$. Thus it is compactly supported $L^2$, while the tail is bounded by $g/L_*$, in joules.

For $s=|x|/L_*\ge1$, $|V_{\mathrm{tail}}(x)|\le(g/L_*)e^{-\mu_*s}$. For any dimensionless $\delta>0$, choose an integer $N>1+\delta$; for $s\ge1$, $(1+s)^{1+\delta}\le(2s)^N$, so [[thm-exponential-beats-every-polynomial]] at $a=\mu_*$ and $m=N$ gives $e^{-\mu_*s}(1+s)^{1+\delta}\to0$. This and continuity on compact intervals give the finite dimensionless constant $C_\delta:=\sup_{s\ge0}e^{-\mu_*s}(1+s)^{1+\delta}$. Hence $|V_{\mathrm{tail}}(x)|\le(g/L_*)C_\delta (1+|x|/L_*)^{-1-\delta}$ on that region; on $|x|<L_*$ the tail is zero, so the bound holds everywhere.

By 1.1 and 2.1 the declared Yukawa potential has the decaying-tail form of [[pthm-nrqm-scattering-resolvent-tail-asymptotic-completeness]] clause (c) with any $\delta>0$; hence, by that theorem, the model's interacting operator is self-adjoint on $W^{2,2}$, its wave operators exist and are asymptotically complete with vanishing singular continuous spectrum, and its scattering operator is unitary.

For each $x\ne0$, as $\mu\to0^{+}$ the potential $V_{g,\mu}(x)$ tends to $-g/|x|$; assigning any value to the limiting Coulomb potential at the origin gives the same multiplication operator. For that limiting potential, and for every split into a compactly supported part and a remainder, the quotient $(1+|x|/L_*)^{1+\delta}|V_{\mathrm{tail}}(x)|=g(1+|x|/L_*)^{1+\delta}/|x|$ tends to $+\infty$ as $|x|\to\infty$ for every $\delta>0$, so the sufficient decay hypothesis of that theorem fails and the Coulomb case is not covered by the short-range class; its treatment is the separate declared long-range model [[def-nrqm-scattering-coulomb-dollard-model]], for which the theorem supplies no ordinary-comparison statement.
